items.content_html:
Program run in cooperation with the Blinken Open Society Archivum Budapest offers research fellowships at the Open Society Archives (OSA) at the Central European University in Budapest.

At-a-Glance Criteria

  • Eligibility & Origin: Anybody holding a MA degree in the social sciences or the humanities; the program is not limited to citizens of V4 countries
  • Research Requirements: Applicants are recommended to refer to at least one of the listed research topics in their application.
  • Duration & funding: The two-month scholarship is €3,000; shorter research periods are pro-rated.

Guidelines & Files

Guideline documents are not available yet.

Timeline

Sep 1, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Call opens

Nov 10, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Final application deadline

Dec 20, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Results announced

Scholarships are awarded two times per year on a com­pet­i­tive basis to scholars, artists or journalists from V4 and non-V4 coun­tries who wish to con­duct research at OSA, and whose cur­rent research projects are rel­e­vant to the hold­ings and the given research pri­or­i­ties of the Fund and OSA. The €3,000 scholarship is designed to pro­vide access to the archives, cover travel to/from Budapest, mod­est sub­sis­tence, and accom­mo­da­tion for a research period of two months. Scholarships for shorter peri­ods are pro-rated.

Altogether, 20 fel­low­ships are awarded annu­ally to selected applicants from V4 coun­tries.

Research theme within the Visegrad Scholarships at OSA in 2026/27: Naming Reality

The words of Václav Havel on the need for truthfulness in times of social conflict returned to public attention in 2026. Politicians and the wider public increasingly began discussing systemic problems within the international order and the relationship between truth and politics. During the Cold War, openly describing reality was often risky or restricted. Official language concealed crises and conflicts through what Havel called “evasive language” — replacing reality with ideological rhetoric.

This call therefore encourages researchers and artists to reflect on how reality was described under conditions of censorship, limited access to information, and political pressure between East and West. On the occasion of the 35th anniversary of the Visegrad Group, it also recalls the efforts of Central European countries after 1989 to rebuild a shared political language grounded in open debate and reliable information.

We invite scientists, researchers, artists, and journalists to reflect on what the “Naming Reality” project can offer and remind us of, including within the following:

  • the content and practices of truth-telling among oppositionists and dissidents;
  • the dilemmas of artistic and literary actors in re-creating socio-political languages that paradoxically eschewed direct engagement with “reality”;
  • cases of ideological disillusionment and awakening among left-wing thinkers and workers and re-evaluation of Marxist concepts regarding “reality”;
  • the strategies of the documentary media: novels, films, private photo collections;
  • the role of transnational cultural organizations in promoting realist and/or aesthetically reflexive works and authors;
  • the tools of empirical realism and its relationship to political thinking;
  • the samizdat cultures of bypassing official channels and documenting phenomena;
  • the workings of propaganda and the dismantlement of the very idea of truth;
  • the usage of political psychiatry against people whose perception of abusive realities was questioned;
  • the status of information within archival cultures of fact-gathering and documentation;
  • critical archiving from the margins (documentation about marginalized communities, racialized or stigmatized identities);
  • transnational networks of information about development behind the Iron Curtain;
  • human rights monitoring and reporting in Socialist states and their connection with Western organizations/exilic communities;
  • the limits and paradoxes of anti-Stalinist prose;
  • the paradoxes of documenting “totalitarianism,” dissent, and protest in the 70s, at the heart of the détente;
  • the Western reception of (un)comfortable truths about Socialism/Communism;
  • the epistemological challenges of expert cultures in times of information and material shortages (the reliability of data and the methods of sociology, statistics, futurology, demography, food engineering within Communism)
  • the afterlives of censored cultural artifacts after the fall of Communism;
  • the post-1989 re-evaluation and verification of systemic socio-political insights from before 1989 (the meta-analysis of their framing, concepts, as well as of their accuracy).

The sub-topics are meant to enable and inspire various reflections on the topic of the call, not to limit the range of possible connected themes and analyses. Potential candidates can refer to them, enrich them, and work with them. Please also mention the collections you would like to consult and be as specific as possible with regards to the sub-fonds and series you might find relevant for your research.

Please direct your questions to the project administrator, Katalin Gadoros.

The application process is run via the OSA website. Deadlines for applications are: 25 July, 15 November.

Application procedure

Please submit the following to OSA:

  1. Application letter in English (should specify expected period of stay and preferred dates). Please note that the Archive’s Research Room is closed during the Christmas period, and the research stay must end on the last day of the given academic year, July 31.
  2. Research description/plan in English (about 800 words and should include the following: introduction, presentation of the stage of research, literature on the subject, preliminary hypothesis, questions, identification of possible documents in the OSA holdings). Artists are expected to submit a portfolio, too.
  3. Curriculum Vitae (C.V.)
  4. Proof of officially recognized advanced level English language exam (native speakers and those with qualification from an English language institution/degree program are exempted)
  5. Names of two referees with contact address. Letters of reference are not needed.

The Application letter, C.V., the Research description/plan, the copy of a language exam certification and the Referees’ contact information should be sent by email to Katalin Gadoros.

• Gulbenkian Orchestra

    In 1962, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation decided to establish a permanent orchestral ensemble. Originally with only twelve musicians (strings and continuo) it was named “Orquestra de Câmara Gulbenkian”. This collective was successively enlarged and today the “Orquestra Gulbenkian” (the name it has adopted since 1971) has a permanent body of sixty instrumentalists, a number that can be expanded depending on the repertoire.

    This structure allows the Gulbenkian Orchestra to interpret works from the Baroque and Classical periods, a significant part of 19th century orchestral literature and much of the music of the 20th century, including works belonging to the current repertoire of the traditional symphonic orchestras. In each season, the orchestra performs on a regular series of concerts at the Gulbenkian Grand Auditorium in Lisbon, where it has had the opportunity of working together with some of leading names of the world of music (conductors and soloists). It has also performed on numerous locations all over Portugal, in an effort to decentralize music and culture.

    The orchestra has been constantly expanding its activities in the international level, performing in Europe, Asia Africa, and the Americas. In the recording field, Orquestra Gulbenkian is associated to labels as Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Hyperion, Teldec, Erato, Adès, Nimbus, Lyrinx, Naïve and Pentatone, among others, and this activity was recognized with several international prizes.

    Hannu Lintu is the Music Director of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2023.

  • Hannu Lintu

    Music Director

    “Dynamic and sharp on the podium” (Bachtrack) and with an ​“extreme clarity of purpose, every detail worth noting” (Los Angeles Times), Hannu Lintu maintains his reputation as one of the world’s finest conductors. This season Lintu continues his tenures as Music Director of Orquestra Gulbenkian and Chief Conductor of Finnish National Opera and Ballet, proving himself a master of both symphonic and operatic repertoire, as well as beginning his tenures as Artistic Partner of the Lahti Symphony Orchestra and Artistic Director of the International Sibelius Festival.

    Last season also saw Lintu’s appointment as Music Director of Singapore Symphony Orchestra from 2026/27, where he will appear this season for several performances, including for Haydn’s Nelson Mass and Shostakovich’s 7th Leningrad Symphony. Other highlights include returns to the BBC, St Louis, Toronto, Baltimore and Detroit Symphonies, as well as productions of Strauss’ Elektra and a world premiere of Sebastian Fagerlund’s The Morning Star at Finnish National Opera.

    Symphonic highlights of recent years have seen Lintu conduct the Chicago Symphony, New York Philharmonic (including an immediate re-invitation from the orchestra to perform at Bravo! Vail Festival), Berliner Philharmoniker, The Cleveland Orchestra, Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra, Orchestre National de Radio France, Boston Symphony Orchestra, Swedish Radio Symphony Orchestra, BBC Symphony, Deutsches Symphonie-Orchester Berlin, Radio Filharmonisch Orkest, London Philharmonic, Atlanta Symphony Orchestra, Konzerthausorchester Berlin, St Louis Symphony, and Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal.

    As an expert in both operatic as well as symphonic repertoire, Lintu’s recent opera highlights have included Enescu’s Œdipe with the Vienna Symphony at Bregenz Festspiele, Wagner’s Der fliegende Holländer at Opera de Paris and Debussy’s Pelléas et Mélisande at Bayerische Staatsoper as a guest conductor, as well as multiple productions at Finnish National Opera and Ballet, including a recent multi-season Ring Cycle, Poulenc’s Dialogues des Carmélites, Mozart’s Don Giovanni, a choregraphed reimagining of Verdi’s Messa da Requiem, Puccini’s Turandot, Richard Strauss’ Salome, and Britten’s Billy Budd.

    Lintu has made several recordings for Ondine, BIS Records, Naxos, Avie Records and Hyperion Records. His diverse discography comprises recordings of Magnus Lindberg’s orchestral works, the complete Beethoven Piano Concertos with Stephen Hough, and Lutoslawski’s Symphonies Nos. 1-4, all with Finnish Radio Symphony Orchestra. His often-gilded work boasts two International Classical Music Awards and several nominations for Gramophone and GRAMMY awards in recognition of recording projects such as Bartók’s Violin Concertos with Christian Tetzlaff, works by Sibelius featuring Anne Sofie von Otter, Rautavaara’s Kaivos, and the Violin Concertos of Sibelius and Thomas Adès with Augustin Hadelich and Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra.

    Lintu studied cello and piano at the Sibelius Academy, where he also later studied conducting with Jorma Panula. He participated in masterclasses with Myung-Whun Chung at L’Accademia Musicale Chigiana in Siena, Italy, and took first prize at the Nordic Conducting Competition in Bergen in 1994.

Mihran Tomasyan and Saro Usta, grew up together in the Kurtulus neighbourhood of Istanbul, sharing the same culture and a strong sense of common identity. In SAR, they use music, movement and paper to bring together their memories, take them apart and piece them back together.

“You chose your seedling, decided on a good place for it, prepared its soil, watered it for the first time, turned your back and walked away, days passed, perhaps weeks, the rains came, and then snow, winds blew, every now and then you came and checked, it had grown to your height, it had held up well, its roots could sink as deep as eternity, then came spring and then came summer, the sun rose, the moon set, Venus came up, you were already dead, who knows where your grandchildren woke up, some had departed, those who arrived had departed from other places, it didn’t work out, some things went wrong, the tree grew, there used to be one house in the distance, then there were three, then five, then five hundred, murders took place in its shade, and of course, some kissed, too, some never realized it stood there, and some gave it water.

Then they chopped it down.

And thank goodness for that because the pavement needed widening.

This performance was constructed upon a misunderstanding of the world, humanity, mountains, the earth and the sky. It has absolutely nothing to do with the tree mentioned above. The performance is interested in knowing where the grandchildren wake up. Enjoy the performance.”

The aim of this grant is to encourage projects that contribute to creating and strengthening international collaboration networks with an impact on the professional growth of the candidate artists as well as the visibility and recognition of their work;

To support the travel of artists/programmers/curators to participate in artistic projects promoted by leading international cultural institutions with regular activity in the areas covered by the open call.

Conditions

The following artistic areas are supported:

  • Performing Arts: dance, theatre and new circus;
  • Visual Arts: drawing, sculpture, photography, performance, painting and video;
  • Cinema: directing;
  • Cross-Disciplinary Projects: projects that integrate at least two different disciplines, the main one being one of the artistic areas defined for the competition (Performing Arts, Visual Arts or Cinema), and cannot focus on the fields of architecture, design, publishing or music.

Eligibility

Who can apply:

  • Portuguese artists, curators and programmers in their individual capacity, or through private Portuguese non-profit organisations with which they collaborate in the implementation of the project. Foreign artists must have tax residency in Portugal and be part of the Portuguese artistic community;
  • Projects must be submitted at least 30 days prior to the date of their execution and must be executed within the period of 12 months following the application;

  • Each artist can only submit only one application per year;

  • Applications will only be accepted online and in Portuguese.

How to Apply

  • Register to apply;

  • Before submitting the application form, check all the eligibility criteria. We advise you to read the Regulations and Frequently Asked Questions (available in the Documents area);

  • Applications can only be submitted once all the mandatory fields of the form have been completed and the documentation required by the Regulation has been uploaded;

  • At the end, click on the 'submit application' button. In order to prevent difficulties in submitting applications, avoid submitting your application in the last few days of the deadline.

Contacts

If you have any questions after consulting the FAQs and the regulations, please contact the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation at [email protected].

Drawing on letters, diaries and archival documents, the film follows Calouste Gulbenkian’s search for a lasting home for the works of art he called his ‘children’—from the Caucasus to Paris, from wartime London to Washington, and finally to Lisbon.

Born in Constantinople, between East and West, Gulbenkian assembled one of the largest private art collections in the world while negotiating with empires and governments. Beyond the myth of ‘Mr Five Per Cent’, the film finds a man absorbed by a more personal question: where, ultimately, does all this art belong?

Shot during the recent renovation of the Gulbenkian Museum, the documentary takes as its thread the recording of an old audio guide found in the empty galleries.

That voice leads us through the life, obsessions and silences of Calouste Sarkis Gulbenkian. Moving between documentary, cinematic reconstruction and observation, the film turns the Museum itself into a character. Drawing on letters, diaries and archival documents, the film follows Calouste Gulbenkian’s search for a lasting home for the works of art he called his ‘children’—from the Caucasus to Paris, from wartime London to Washington, and finally to Lisbon.

Born in Constantinople, between East and West, Gulbenkian assembled one of the largest private art collections in the world while negotiating with empires and governments. Beyond the myth of ‘Mr Five Per Cent’, the film finds a man absorbed by a more personal question: where, ultimately, does all this art belong?

Shot during the recent renovation of the Gulbenkian Museum, the documentary takes as its thread the recording of an old audio guide found in the empty galleries.

That voice leads us through the life, obsessions and silences of Calouste Sarkis Gulbenkian. Moving between documentary, cinematic reconstruction and observation, the film turns the Museum itself into a character. As the works are taken down, packed and reinstalled, the building takes over as narrator, telling the story of a man who refused interviews, avoided cameras and left almost no record of his image or voice.

A film about art, exile and belonging—and about what museums hold beyond their objects.

Commissioned by the Gulbenkian Foundation for its 70th anniversary.

• Marlene Monteiro Freitas

    Marlene Monteiro Freitas (1979, Cape Verde) is known for creating pieces whose hallmark is openness, hybridity, impurity and intensity. She has won numerous awards, including the Silver Lion at the Venice Biennale (2020), the Chanel Next Prize (2021) and the Evens Arts Prize (2022). Since 2020, she has been a co-curator of the (un)common ground project.

  • Nuno Barreto

    Nuno Barreto, from Praia, Cape Verde, has been a dancer for more than 20 years and is a cultural activist. He is part of the dance company Raiz di Polon, through which he has participated in tours of Europe, America and Asia. He has performed and choreographed the pieces: Linhas di Kommuni, Torna Liga, Dos Porta, Cisne Pretu, Stratus di sociedadi, Izulamentu20, Ken Ke Mi, and Kontra Tempu, among others. He is a mentor for the project Badju KaBu Kabu and the Festival Cabo Verde Dança.

  • Djam Neguin

    Djam Neguin is one of the most prominent and revolutionary figures on today’s Cape Verdean arts and culture scene. A multidisciplinary artist, his unique career stands out for his many talents and feats in the areas of dance, music, theatre, fashion, performance, literature, and audiovisual, which also complement his activities as a producer and activist.

  • Rosy Timas

    Rosy Timas is a Cape Verdean dancer and co-creator. She started her career in 1999 with the company Raiz di Polon. With six solo works and performances in more than 40 countries, she has participated in and led countless workshops. Her art reflects the depth of her experiences and her vision of the world. She is devoted to capturing beauty in every movement, using dance as a form of connection and expression.

  • Pak Ndjamena

    Pak Ndjamena, from Maputo, Mozambique, is a dancer, choreographer, contemporary dance teacher, actor, and director of contemporary dance and music films, and has developed a series of hybrid dance techniques. He has choreographed and performed more than 20 pieces and won the Mozal Arts and Culture Award 2019, in the category of dance, in Maputo. He has led workshops for the Tremuria Project and performed at renowned international festivals.

  • Francisca Mirine

    Francisca Mirine is a Mozambican dancer, performer, dance teacher and choreographer. She has worked with national and international artists and participated in festivals, workshops, dance creations and artistic residencies and exchange programmes. She devises her own dance creations and writes her own projects. She regards herself as an independent artist.

• Gulbenkian Orchestra

    In 1962, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation decided to establish a permanent orchestral ensemble. Originally with only twelve musicians (strings and continuo) it was named “Orquestra de Câmara Gulbenkian”. This collective was successively enlarged and today the “Orquestra Gulbenkian” (the name it has adopted since 1971) has a permanent body of sixty instrumentalists, a number that can be expanded depending on the repertoire.

    This structure allows the Gulbenkian Orchestra to interpret works from the Baroque and Classical periods, a significant part of 19th century orchestral literature and much of the music of the 20th century, including works belonging to the current repertoire of the traditional symphonic orchestras. In each season, the orchestra performs on a regular series of concerts at the Gulbenkian Grand Auditorium in Lisbon, where it has had the opportunity of working together with some of leading names of the world of music (conductors and soloists). It has also performed on numerous locations all over Portugal, in an effort to decentralize music and culture.

    The orchestra has been constantly expanding its activities in the international level, performing in Europe, Asia Africa, and the Americas. In the recording field, Orquestra Gulbenkian is associated to labels as Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Hyperion, Teldec, Erato, Adès, Nimbus, Lyrinx, Naïve and Pentatone, among others, and this activity was recognized with several international prizes.

    Hannu Lintu is the Music Director of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2023.

  • Nuno Coelho

    Conductor

    Nuno has been Chief Conductor and Artistic Director of Spain’s Orquesta Sinfónica del Principado de Asturias since October 2022. In addition to concerts in Oviedo, the 2024/25 season sees him return to Antwerp Symphony, Tampere Philharmonic, Gulbenkian Orchestra and Orquesta Sinfónica de RTVE, and debut with Stavanger Symphony, Staatsphilharmonie Nürnberg and Minnesota Orchestra.

    Highlights of recent seasons have included concerts with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, BBC Scottish Symphony, Netherlands Radio Philharmonic, Frankfurt’s hr-Sinfonieorchester, Orquestra Sinfônica de São Paulo, Orquesta Nacional de España, Dresden Philharmonie, Orchestre Philharmonique du Luxembourg, Orchestre Philharmonique Royal de Liège, Residentie Orkest, Orchestre philharmonique de Strasbourg, Orquesta Sinfonica de Galicia, and Orquestra Simfónica de Barcelona.

    In the opera pit, Nuno has conducted productions of La traviata, Cavalleria rusticana, Rusalka and Manon. In November 2022 he conducted his own staging of José Saramago’s reimagining of Don Giovanni at the Gulbenkian, having previously conducted their semi-staging of Così fan tutte the previous season. 2026 will see Nuno return to Ópera de Oviedo for Manon Lescaut.

    Nuno won First Prize at the 2017 Cadaqués International Conducting Competition and has since gone on to conduct the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic, BBC Philharmonic, Symphoniker Hamburg, Orquesta Sinfónica de Castilla y León, Noord Nederlands Orkest and Orchestra Teatro Regio Torino. He was a Los Angeles Philharmonic Dudamel Fellow between 2018-19 and stepped in for Bernard Haitink that same season to make his debut with the Symphonieorchester des Bayerischen Rundfunks.

    Born in Porto, Nuno studied conducting at the Zürich University of the Arts with Johannes Schlaefli and won the Neeme Järvi Prize at the Gstaad Menuhin Festival. In 2015 he was admitted into the German Music Council’s Dirigentenforum and for the following two years he was both a Tanglewood Conducting Fellow and Assistant Conductor of the Netherlands Philharmonic.

    Literature and tennis occupy his time off-podium.

The Gulbenkian Foundation and Imprensa Nacional-Casa da Moeda (INCM) present a €2 coin marking the institution’s 70th anniversary (1956–2026).

The national side, designed by Pedro Carvalho, shows the quadriga—a chariot drawn by four horses and the institution’s emblem—representing its four statutory purposes: Art, Charity, Science and Education. The design also recalls the extensive collection of Greco-Roman coins assembled by Calouste Gulbenkian.

The coin is issued as a circulation coin, legal tender throughout the euro area, and in special-finish editions for collectors.

    This structure allows the Gulbenkian Orchestra to interpret works from the Baroque and Classical periods, a significant part of 19th century orchestral literature and much of the music of the 20th century, including works belonging to the current repertoire of the traditional symphonic orchestras. In each season, the orchestra performs on a regular series of concerts at the Gulbenkian Grand Auditorium in Lisbon, where it has had the opportunity of working together with some of leading names of the world of music (conductors and soloists). It has also performed on numerous locations all over Portugal, in an effort to decentralize music and culture.

    The orchestra has been constantly expanding its activities in the international level, performing in Europe, Asia Africa, and the Americas. In the recording field, Orquestra Gulbenkian is associated to labels as Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Hyperion, Teldec, Erato, Adès, Nimbus, Lyrinx, Naïve and Pentatone, among others, and this activity was recognized with several international prizes.

    Hannu Lintu is the Music Director of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2023.

  • Mariano Chiacchiarini

    Conductor

    Recognized by critics worldwide with the ECHO Music Prize, the German Record Critics' Award, and the KONEX Prize in Music, Mariano began his international career by winning the 1st prize at the Teatro Colón Conducting Competition. This led to collaborations with the most prominent conductors, such as Sir S. Rattle, P. Boulez, P. Eötvös, R. Chailly, R. Muti, and B. Haitink; and to work with the most renowned orchestras and ensembles, including the Hong Kong Phil, Filarmonica della Scala, Orchestra della Svizzera Italiana, Russian State Orchestra, Philharmonique de Radio France, WDR Sinfonieorchester, German Radio Phil, Gulbenkian Orquestra and the Stuttgarter Philharmoniker. He has been invited to major festivals and concert venues, including the Lucerne Festival, Schleswig-Holstein Music Festival, Young Euro Classic, Donaueschinger Musiktage, Elbphilharmonie, Konzerthaus Vienna and Berlin, Tchaikovsky Hall Moscow, Teatro Colón, Deutsche Oper am Rhein and l’Opéra Bastille. Mariano has served as Music Director of Trier University, as Conductor of Ensemble Garage and since 2014 began his cooperation with the National Symphony in Argentina. Most recently he was selected by Barbara Hannigan’s Momentum Project, named as a member of the German Music Council, as “Outstanding Personality of the Culture” of his hometown and awarded with the Premio Nacional Clásica. In 2025, he received the Music Critics Association Award as “Conductor of the Year” at the Parliament of Buenos Aires.

    Since 2022 Mariano Chiacchiarini was chosen Universitätsmusikdirektor of the city of Bremen.

  • Alice Caplow-Sparks

    Oboe / Cor anglais

    Alice Caplow-Sparks began playing oboe at the age of twelve in her hometown of Seattle. She continued her studies in Mexico City for a year, then returning to Seattle where she was a student of the oboist Alex Klein. At the age of eighteen, she left Seattle to pursue her studies at the Oberlin Conservatory in Ohio with James Caldwell. During her time there, she was actively involved with the Oberlin Contemporary Music Ensemble, as well as other chamber music ensembles and orchestras. Her keen interest in chamber music first developed during a tour of Paris with the Oberlin Woodwind Quintet. After completing her degree, she entered the Eastman School of Music in Rochester, New York, where she attended classes and completed her Masters with Richard Killmer. While at Eastman, she commissioned an original work for oboe and string trio from the composer Gregory Mertl, which she premièred in her graduation recital. She then travelled to Paris, where she studied with David Walter at the Conservatoire. In 2004, she joined the Orquestra Metropolitana de Lisboa and she is currently a member of the Gulbenkian Orchestra, where she has played oboe and English horn since 2006.

  • José Pedro Pereira

    Trumpet

    José Pedro Pereira was born in 1998. He is trumpet B soloist at the Gulbenkian Orchestra. He initiated his piano and trumpet studies at the Conservatório de Música de Felgueiras, later continuing his training at the Academia José Atalaya in Fafe. In 2010, he enrolled at the Escola Profissional Artística do Vale do Ave where he studied under Paulo Silva and graduated with top marks. In 2016, he was admitted into the Zürcher Hochschule der Künste – Zurich, where he studied under Frits Damrow and Laurent Tinguely and also, for Baroque trumpet, under Simon Lilly.

    During his training, he took countless advanced courses with Pierre Dutot, Frits Damrow, Mark David, Pasi Pirinen, Philippe Litzler, Pacho Flores, Konradin Groth, Reinhold Friedrich, Jeroen Berwaerts, Philip Smith and Sergei Nakariakov, among others.

    He has won awards in Portuguese and international competitions, including the Eric Aubier International Trumpet Competition (France), Internationaler Bodensee Musikwettbewerb (Germany), “Terras de La Salette” Wind Instruments International Competition, Póvoa de Varzim Trumpet Competition, Rubén Simeó International Trumpet Competition and the Albertino Lucas Luso-Galician Competition. In 2018, he won 1st Prize (advanced level) at the 32nd Young Musicians Awards.

    He was a student musician at the Opernaus Zürich / Philharmonia Zürich (2019–2022), where he worked with innumerable internationally renowned conductors and singers. In the role of soloist, he has played for the Gulbenkian Orchestra, Orchestre de l‘Opéra de Rouen Normandie, Südwestdeutsches Kammerorchester Pforzheim and the Banda Sinfónica Portuguesa.

Fashion Residency Program in Milan (IT) opens unique opportunities for professionals and researchers from the Visegrad countries from the field of fashion, design and related areas. An experience based in Milan, the heart of the fashion industry, for two months with the possibility of visits to Rome as well. Research and "live fashion" within the context of individual exploration supported by lectures and experiences with Accademia Costume & Moda.

At-a-Glance Criteria

  • Eligibility: Applicants V4 citizens, age 18+, good written/spoken English (Italian is a plus).
  • Applicants may come from fashion or non-fashion backgrounds and showing a clear interest in the Italian fashion supply chain.
  • Selection criteria: A creative approach demonstrated by previous work/projects plus residency plan, and a defined research proposal.
  • Timing: lasting June 1 – July 31 in Milan, Italy
  • Funding: €6,000 per artist to cover living expenses.

Guidelines & Files

Timeline

Sep 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Call opens

Oct 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Final application deadline

Dec 20, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Results announced

Jun 1, 2027 at 9:00 AM: Project start

Accademia Costume & Moda (ACM) has a long tradition in educating professionals in  the areas of Fashion, Costume for the Performing Arts, Communication and Management.

Founded in 1964 in Rome by Rosana Pistolese, costume and fashion historian, as well as costume designer for theater, television and cinema, and also fashion and costume writer and publicist.

Thanks to the great talent and passion of its founder, Accademia has become over time a laboratory of ideas and research. An Italian prestigious private academy and cultural association that offers unique resources to carry out varied research within the wider scope of the fashion industry.

During the Fashion Residency in Milan, four selected professionals, with a background or an interest in the broad field of fashion, access to a campus studio designed for creative work, research and networking. Participant will receive individual as well as group guidance with lectures and discussions regarding topics such as Contemporary Art, Fashion History, Sociology, Understanding Contemporary Fashion, Portfolio Building and Communication, as well as others.

Fashion Residents will get series of lectures about art & fashion, fashion & society, fashion fabrics history, knitwear history and industry overview, and special masterclass about fashion design & production ethics too. They will also take part in planned visits to museums and cultural institutions as well as possible trade fairs. To enhance the research and educational support, access to Luigi Bocconi Library is granted and a special excursion to the seat of AMC in Rome is included too.

During the residency the main emphasis is on research projects. However, there is also a program aimed at enriching and supporting your experience. It is unique research practice involvement between the Accademia, museums, libraries, archives, industry initiatives and exhibitions. Together they create a rich tapestry of knowledge gathering, inspiration and in-depth research.

Individuals who have a passion for fashion whether they are artists, designers or researchers are welcome although with no background in fashion design. The goal is to embrace diversity in applications and reach out to artists, digital artists, designers and communicators interested in understanding the Italian Fashion System and Supply Chain.

Join an unique opportunity that combines peer learning with an experience during Fashion residency in Milan!

Fashion Residency Program in Milan (IT) opens unique opportunities for professionals and researchers from the Visegrad countries from the field of fashion, design and related areas. An experience based in Milan, the heart of the fashion industry, for two months with the possibility of visits to Rome as well. Research and "live fashion" within the context of individual exploration supported by lectures and experiences with Accademia Costume & Moda.

At-a-Glance Criteria

  • Eligibility: Applicants V4 citizens, age 18+, good written/spoken English (Italian is a plus).
  • Applicants may come from fashion or non-fashion backgrounds and showing a clear interest in the Italian fashion supply chain.
  • Selection criteria: A creative approach demonstrated by previous work/projects plus residency plan, and a defined research proposal.
  • Timing: lasting June 1 – July 31 in Milan, Italy
  • Funding: €6,000 per artist to cover living expenses.

Guidelines & Files

Accademia Costume & Moda (ACM) has a long tradition in educating professionals in  the areas of Fashion, Costume for the Performing Arts, Communication and Management.

Founded in 1964 in Rome by Rosana Pistolese, costume and fashion historian, as well as costume designer for theater, television and cinema, and also fashion and costume writer and publicist.

Thanks to the great talent and passion of its founder, Accademia has become over time a laboratory of ideas and research. An Italian prestigious private academy and cultural association that offers unique resources to carry out varied research within the wider scope of the fashion industry.

During the Fashion Residency in Milan, four selected professionals, with a background or an interest in the broad field of fashion, access to a campus studio designed for creative work, research and networking. Participant will receive individual as well as group guidance with lectures and discussions regarding topics such as Contemporary Art, Fashion History, Sociology, Understanding Contemporary Fashion, Portfolio Building and Communication, as well as others.

Fashion Residents will get series of lectures about art & fashion, fashion & society, fashion fabrics history, knitwear history and industry overview, and special masterclass about fashion design & production ethics too. They will also take part in planned visits to museums and cultural institutions as well as possible trade fairs. To enhance the research and educational support, access to Luigi Bocconi Library is granted and a special excursion to the seat of AMC in Rome is included too.

During the residency the main emphasis is on research projects. However, there is also a program aimed at enriching and supporting your experience. It is unique research practice involvement between the Accademia, museums, libraries, archives, industry initiatives and exhibitions. Together they create a rich tapestry of knowledge gathering, inspiration and in-depth research.

Literary residencies are intended to develop and promote V4 literature by providing support to the work and mobility of talented writers of fiction and non-fiction, poets, essayists, critics as well as literary translators, publicists and journalists from V4 countries by creating a platform for literary exchanges.

At-a-Glance Criteria

  • Program structure: The program supports Literary Residents hosted by 4 institutions, with residencies held either in Spring or in Autumn Edition.
  • Eligibility & composition: Participants from V4 countries, hosted by an institution, working on individual literary projects while participating in joint literary events.
  • Funding: €1,300 for Spring Edition and €2,600 for Autumn Edition.

Guidelines & Files

Timeline

Sep 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Call opens

Oct 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Final application deadline

Dec 20, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Results announced

May 1, 2027 at 12:00 PM: Project start

The Visegrad Literary Residency Program, consists of a series of residency stays and literary events addressed to writers of fiction and non-fiction, poets, essayists, critics as well as literary translators, publicists and journalists from the Visegrad Countries (Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia). The Villa Decius Association acts as the Coordinator of the Program.

It is based on a partnership of 4 Host Institutions, one in each V4 country: 

Národní institut pro kulturu (Czech Cultural Institute, previously Arts and Theatre Institute) in Prague

Petőfi Irodalmi Múzeum (Petőfi Literary Museum) in Budapest, 

Stowarzyszenie Willa Decjusza (Villa Decius Association) in Krakow and 

Slovenské literárne centrum (Slovak Literary Centre) in Bratislava.

The Program will provide opportunities to host from and in all V4 member states and support work and mobility of talented Literary Residents, to create a platform for information exchange and to support development and promotion of the V4 literature in Central Europe.

Program will enable 32 Literary Residents to carry their literary projects in 4 Host Institutions in one of the given periods: 1st May – 12th June (Compact Spring Edition) or 1st September – 30th November (Regular Autumn Edition).

Each of the Host Institutions will be responsible for organizing two stays of two groups of 4 Literary Residents each (one from the Czechia, one from Hungary, one from Poland and one from Slovakia), who will be working on their individual literary projects, and also participate together in literary event(s) organized in the hosting city by the Host Institution.

The recruitment process of 32 grantees of the Program (8 from the Czech Republic, 8 from Hungary, 8 from Poland and 8 Slovakia) will be based on individual applications submitted via an online application form. For more information on the conditions and implementation of stays in residences, please refer to the Literary Residencies Criteria.

The residences will be assigned to applicants in a 3 stage selection process by a national and international Selection Panel on the basis of proportional and equal involvement of Czech, Hungarian, Polish and Slovak residents and Host Institutions.

Questions regarding the Literary Residency Program should be addressed to Pawel Lyzwiński and technical problems with online application address to Darina Madleňáková.

  • The 2027 edition of the Program will enable 32 Literary Residents to carry their literary projects in 4 Host Institutions in one of the given periods: 1st May – 12th June 2027 (Compact Spring Edition) or 1st September – 30th November 2027 (Regular Autumn Edition).
  • The amount of support is €1,300 for the Compact Spring Edition and €2,600 for Regular Autumn Edition.
  • Each of the Host Institutions will be responsible for organizing two stays of two groups of 4 Literary Residents each (one from the Czech Republic, one from Hungary, one from Poland and one from Slovakia), who will be working on their individual literary projects, and also participate together in literary event(s) organized in the hosting city by the Host Institution.

For more information on the conditions and implementation of stays in residences, please refer to the Literary Residencies Criteria.

The application form must be submitted via My Visegrad by October 15 at 12.00 PM (noon). The online application system opens on September 15.

Each applicant has to fill in the on-line application form (in English) containing:

• Copy of your ID or passport

• Description of the literary plans for the residency

Each applicant may attach other documents, recommendations etc. (in English) which she/he finds important for evaluating her/his application.

items.content_html:
Performing Artist Residencies support contemporary theater and dance in Central Europe by providing opportunities to host artists and companies from/in V4 countries.

At-a-Glance Criteria

  • Eligibility & Scope: Applicants V4 citizens aged 18+, both individual artists and groups, may apply. The residency must take place in a V4 country other than the applicant’s country of citizenship/residence.
  • Artistic Focus & Timing: Supporting experimental and innovative performing arts and excludes stone theaters, finished productions, and festivals.
  • Funding: Residencies last 1 month; individual residency: €2,500 for the artist + €2,000 for the host institution. Group residency: €5,500 for group members + €3,500 for the host institution.

Guidelines & Files

Timeline

Sep 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Call opens

Oct 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Final application deadline

Dec 20, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Results announced

Jan 10, 2027 at 12:00 PM: Project start

Performing Artist residencies support innovation, experiment and creativity in the performing arts – new drama, contemporary dance, new circus, physical theatre, visual theater, alternative theater, performance art. The program is not suitable for stone theaters, already developed performances, or theater festivals.

  • Both individual artists and artistic groups can apply for this type of support
  • The applicant/s must be citizen from V4 country over the age of 18
  • Applicants for group residencies (3 artists or more) may come from different V4 countries (group members, however, must come from V4 countries other than the destination country)
  • The place of residency must be different than the applicant’s citizenship and residence
  • Each applicant can get support only once per calendar year
  • The length of support is 1 month
  • Residencies can take place between January 10 to December 31
  • The support for individual residency is €2,000 for the host institution and €2,500  for the artist
  • The amount of support for group residency is €3,500 for the host institution and €5,500 for the group members

For more information about general conditions and selection criteria, read Rules of the Visegrad Artist Residency Program.

The Final report is to be submitted by the artist and the host institution no later than 30 days after the end of the residency at the latest. The Final reports should be prepared with the help of the questionnaires.

To ensure the timely disbursement of the final installment, residents are kindly requested to complete the Questionnaire within 30 days after the conclusion of their residency. The questionnaire is completed through my.visegrad.org system.

Additionally, residents are required to upload images captured during their residency and provide web links to any related posts.

The host organization is responsible for completing, printing, and signing separate questionnaire. Following this, residents are kindly requested to upload completed questionnaire from the host organization (pdf file) as part of their Final Report through the my.visegrad.org system and submit the whole report. 

Technical problems with online application and other questions should be addressed to Project Manager Lenka Bučková.

The application form must be submitted via My Visegrad by October 15 at 12.00 PM (noon). The online application system opens on September 15 at noon.

Application must be submitted with the following documents:

  • Copy of your ID or passport (of each applicant if applying as a group)
  • Artistic portfolio includes reference and an active link to your performing video
  • Scan of letter of acceptance from the host organization in English on a letterhead paper no older than 3 months which includes the names of the artists; title of the project; planned dates of the residency; date; name and signature of the statutory representative

Throughout the performance, what initially appears to be a game gradually transforms into a surveillance system. Every gesture is recorded; every choice is absorbed; every mistake becomes part of the machine’s own logic. However, at a certain point, that logic breaks down—an unexpected presence alters the functioning of the space, fragmenting the language and turning the bodies into vehicles for a voice whose origin remains undefined.

Sound, light, fog, lasers, and movement interplay to create an environment of constant instability, where technology ceases to function merely as a theatrical tool and ultimately becomes an integral part of the experience. Blurring the lines between performance, installation, and sound composition, ‘AXIOM CASINO’ presents a space where the boundaries between control, perception, and transformation are in constant flux.

Seats for people with reduced mobility, who uses a wheelchair, are available. They must be purchased in person, at our ticket office or by telephone.

items.content_html:
WALANDAWE - A year-long investigation traces nickel from deforested forests and Indigenous land in Sulawesi through China’s battery industry to Volkswagen’s electric cars in Europe, exposing the hidden environmental cost of the green transition.

A year-long investigation traces a nickel supply chain from the forests of Sulawesi, Indonesia, through Chinese refineries and battery manufacturers, to Volkswagen electric vehicles sold across Europe. The reporting centres on the Cahaya and Hengjaya mining concessions, whose output feeds Huayou’s processing operations in Morowali, and examines documented commercial links connecting Huayou to CATL and CATL to Volkswagen.

The investigation combines field reporting with satellite analysis, corporate disclosures and trade records to assess the environmental and social consequences of mining expansion. It finds extensive forest loss linked to nickel extraction, including primary forest and areas of high biodiversity and carbon value. The investigation also documents the impact on the Tolaki Indigenous community, whose traditional livelihoods and collective farmland have been increasingly affected by mining, while a promised local smelter and its expected economic benefits failed to materialise.

At the downstream end, the investigation scrutinises Volkswagen’s claims that its supply chains are protected against deforestation and environmental harm. Volkswagen told reporters it could not rule out that the companies identified might be within its supply chain, but did not disclose specific sourcing arrangements. The investigation does not claim to have physically traced individual nickel molecules into specific battery cells; rather, it establishes a documented chain of commercial and supply relationships linking the mines to Volkswagen through Huayou and CATL. It also raises broader questions about corporate due diligence, supply-chain transparency and the environmental costs of the global transition to electric mobility.

Key findings

  • Nickel mining linked to Volkswagen’s wider supply chain has caused extensive forest loss. TreeMap attributed approximately 1,490 hectares of forest loss within the Cahaya concession since 2001 to nickel mining; at Hengjaya, mining accounted for 772 hectares.
  • The two concessions potentially linked to Volkswagen’s nickel supply chain lost nearly 2,360 hectares of canopy cover, according to the investigation’s analysis.
  • The investigation found a documented supply-chain network linking Cahaya and Hengjaya to Volkswagen through Huayou and CATL. Volkswagen said it could not rule out that the identified companies were in its supply chain.
  • In 2024, Cahaya delivered 11 million tonnes of limonite, almost all of its production, to Huayou’s Morowali smelter; deliveries rose to nearly 12.5 million tonnes in 2025.
  • The investigation documented major environmental risks, including threats to primary forests, high-value carbon sinks and habitat for endangered anoa.
  • The Tolaki community reports losing forests, traditional sources of income and farmland, while the local smelter and development benefits promised in connection with the mining project did not materialise.
  • Volkswagen’s supply-chain controls have significant transparency gaps. The company said it uses satellite monitoring and audits but declined to disclose their results; existing smelter-focused audits do not necessarily establish whether upstream mines are free from deforestation.
  • The investigation raises questions about the climate accounting of EV supply chains, because neither Volkswagen nor its certifier confirmed that emissions from mining-related forest loss were included in the relevant life-cycle assessment.

Methodology

The investigation used a mixed-method, cross-border reporting approach over the course of a year. Reporters conducted on-the-ground interviews and observations in Sulawesi, including with Tolaki community members, local officials, former company personnel, drivers and environmental experts. These findings were combined with satellite and geospatial analysis by specialist organisations, including TreeMap, as well as forest and biodiversity data. The supply chain was reconstructed through corporate annual reports, regulatory filings, shareholder disclosures, official company documents and import-export and shipping records covering principally 2024 and 2025. Reporters cross-checked commercial relationships at successive stages: mining in Cahaya and Hengjaya; processing by Huayou in Indonesia; refining and cathode production in China; battery production by CATL; and deliveries and battery-pack assembly involving Volkswagen. The investigation explicitly distinguishes between documented supply-chain links and physical traceability: no material evidence conclusively proves that nickel from these two mines was incorporated into a specific CATL battery cell shipped to Volkswagen. items.summary:
WALANDAWE - A year-long investigation traces nickel from deforested forests and Indigenous land in Sulawesi through China’s battery industry to Volkswagen’s electric cars in Europe, exposing the hidden environmental cost of the green transition.

A year-long investigation traces a nickel supply chain from the forests of Sulawesi, Indonesia, through Chinese refineries and battery manufacturers, to Volkswagen electric vehicles sold across Europe. The reporting centres on the Cahaya and Hengjaya mining concessions, whose output feeds Huayou’s processing operations in Morowali, and examines documented commercial links connecting Huayou to CATL and CATL to Volkswagen.

The investigation combines field reporting with satellite analysis, corporate disclosures and trade records to assess the environmental and social consequences of mining expansion. It finds extensive forest loss linked to nickel extraction, including primary forest and areas of high biodiversity and carbon value. The investigation also documents the impact on the Tolaki Indigenous community, whose traditional livelihoods and collective farmland have been increasingly affected by mining, while a promised local smelter and its expected economic benefits failed to materialise.

At the downstream end, the investigation scrutinises Volkswagen’s claims that its supply chains are protected against deforestation and environmental harm. Volkswagen told reporters it could not rule out that the companies identified might be within its supply chain, but did not disclose specific sourcing arrangements. The investigation does not claim to have physically traced individual nickel molecules into specific battery cells; rather, it establishes a documented chain of commercial and supply relationships linking the mines to Volkswagen through Huayou and CATL. It also raises broader questions about corporate due diligence, supply-chain transparency and the environmental costs of the global transition to electric mobility.

Key findings

  • Nickel mining linked to Volkswagen’s wider supply chain has caused extensive forest loss. TreeMap attributed approximately 1,490 hectares of forest loss within the Cahaya concession since 2001 to nickel mining; at Hengjaya, mining accounted for 772 hectares.
  • The two concessions potentially linked to Volkswagen’s nickel supply chain lost nearly 2,360 hectares of canopy cover, according to the investigation’s analysis.
  • The investigation found a documented supply-chain network linking Cahaya and Hengjaya to Volkswagen through Huayou and CATL. Volkswagen said it could not rule out that the identified companies were in its supply chain.
  • In 2024, Cahaya delivered 11 million tonnes of limonite, almost all of its production, to Huayou’s Morowali smelter; deliveries rose to nearly 12.5 million tonnes in 2025.
  • The investigation documented major environmental risks, including threats to primary forests, high-value carbon sinks and habitat for endangered anoa.
  • The Tolaki community reports losing forests, traditional sources of income and farmland, while the local smelter and development benefits promised in connection with the mining project did not materialise.
  • Volkswagen’s supply-chain controls have significant transparency gaps. The company said it uses satellite monitoring and audits but declined to disclose their results; existing smelter-focused audits do not necessarily establish whether upstream mines are free from deforestation.
  • The investigation raises questions about the climate accounting of EV supply chains, because neither Volkswagen nor its certifier confirmed that emissions from mining-related forest loss were included in the relevant life-cycle assessment.

Methodology

The investigation used a mixed-method, cross-border reporting approach over the course of a year. Reporters conducted on-the-ground interviews and observations in Sulawesi, including with Tolaki community members, local officials, former company personnel, drivers and environmental experts. These findings were combined with satellite and geospatial analysis by specialist organisations, including TreeMap, as well as forest and biodiversity data. The supply chain was reconstructed through corporate annual reports, regulatory filings, shareholder disclosures, official company documents and import-export and shipping records covering principally 2024 and 2025. Reporters cross-checked commercial relationships at successive stages: mining in Cahaya and Hengjaya; processing by Huayou in Indonesia; refining and cathode production in China; battery production by CATL; and deliveries and battery-pack assembly involving Volkswagen. The investigation explicitly distinguishes between documented supply-chain links and physical traceability: no material evidence conclusively proves that nickel from these two mines was incorporated into a specific CATL battery cell shipped to Volkswagen. Companies and relevant authorities were approached for comment, and their responses or refusals to provide details were incorporated into the reporting.

NEW YORK – Today, the Ford Foundation announced the election of Fatima Goss Graves to its board of trustees. Ms. Goss Graves is the president and chief executive officer of the National Women’s Law Center and president of the National Women’s Law Center Action Fund. 

“We are thrilled to welcome Fatima Goss Graves’s perspective and expertise to the Ford Foundation Board of Trustees,” said Ursula Burns, Chair of the Ford Foundation Board of Trustees. “Fatima’s track record speaks for itself, her strategic vision, fearless advocacy, and proven ability to drive meaningful organizational and systemic change make her an invaluable addition to our Board of Trustees.”

Ms. Goss Graves is a nationally recognized expert on gender justice, law, policy, and culture change. As an attorney, she has spent her career fighting to advance opportunities for women and girls, including income security and COVID relief, equal pay, health and reproductive rights, education access, workplace justice and ending sexual harassment and violence – with a focus on women and girls of color. 

“Fatima Goss Graves possesses a sharp legal intellect, exceptional sector insight, and a steadfast dedication to justice,” said Heather Gerken, president of the Ford Foundation. “I could not be more excited to welcome her to the Board of Trustees. Across Fatima’s career, her strategic vision and formidable advocacy have broadened pathways for communities everywhere, particularly women and girls of color. Her presence and insights will be invaluable as we enter the next chapter of the Ford Foundation.”

“I am deeply honored to join the Board of Trustees and work alongside the Ford Foundation’s extraordinary leadership,” said Fatima Goss Graves. “I have dedicated my career to ensuring that all people can live with safety, dignity, and full agency over their lives and that women and their families have what they need to flourish. I am eager to bring that same commitment to Ford’s vital mission in the years ahead.”

Ms. Goss Graves has testified on complex policy matters at the state and federal levels of government in the United States and has been legal and social commentator on CBS, MSNBC, BBC, CNN, PBS, and NPR, and numerous outlets, including the New York Times, Wall Street Journal and the Washington Post. 

In addition to the Ford Foundation, Ms. Goss Graves serves on a number of boards in advisory and governance capacities. Based in Washington D.C., she is a graduate of UCLA and Yale Law School. 

Ford Foundation trustees are elected by the board and serve six-year terms. Trustees set broad policies relating to grantmaking, geographic focus, investments, governance, and professional standards, and they oversee independent audits. The foundation’s trustees come from around the world and have extensive experience in higher education, business and finance, technology, law, government, civil society, and the nonprofit sector.

The Ford Foundation

The Ford Foundation is an independent organization working to address inequality and build a future grounded in justice. For 90 years, it has supported visionaries on the frontlines of social change worldwide, guided by its mission to strengthen democratic values, reduce poverty and injustice, promote international cooperation, and advance human achievement. Today, with an endowment of $18 billion, the foundation has headquarters in New York and 10 regional offices across Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. Artichoke Credit Union, designed with and for the disability community, will aim to increase financial inclusion for people with disabilities, who often face unique challenges in the financial services marketplace. 

NEW YORK – The Ford Foundation, the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation (RWJF) today announced joint funding to launch a credit union to serve people with disabilities. Artichoke Credit Union is a sub-brand created in partnership with Michigan State University Federal Credit Union (MSUFCU) and is designed to center the needs, voices, and experiences of the disability community, with the goal of increasing financial inclusion for people with disabilities. 

Artichoke Credit Union, the first credit union of its kind, is designed to serve people with disabilities, their families, caregivers, advocates, and supporting organizations nationwide. Artichoke Credit Union is expected to begin accepting member sign-ups in the early second quarter of 2027.

The name Artichoke Credit Union is inspired by Ed Roberts, a pioneer in the independent living movement. When Roberts, who contracted polio at age 14, overheard a doctor tell his mother that he would be a “vegetable” if he survived the illness, Roberts declared that he “decided to be an artichoke—a little prickly on the outside but with a big heart.” Roberts was also the first MacArthur Fellow with a disability. 

The foundations, all of which are members of the President’s Council on Disability Inclusion in Philanthropy, are announcing the launch today at a Ford Foundation-led disability economic summit at Gallaudet University in Washington, D.C. 

“A thriving democracy depends on economic inclusion, yet millions of Americans with disabilities cannot access the financial tools needed to build assets and secure their independence,” said Heather Gerken, president of the Ford Foundation. “The Ford Foundation is proud to partner with the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, and Michigan State University Federal Credit Union, to support Artichoke Credit Union. Artichoke Credit Union is designed by and for the disability community and exemplifies the structural changes needed to dismantle systemic barriers, expand access, and restore economic agency for every individual.”

“Artichoke Credit Union highlights what we can achieve when we prioritize disability inclusion,” said John Palfrey, president of the MacArthur Foundation. “When we listen to the disability community to understand their needs and incorporate their perspectives, we can build institutions that better serve everyone.”

“Health and financial well-being are inextricably linked. Achieving health equity is only possible if we work together to build a more inclusive economy,” said Richard Besser, MD, president and CEO of RWJF. “Artichoke Credit Union will help tear down persistent barriers to financial stability for people with disabilities, creating pathways for dignity, financial freedom, and, ultimately, better health.” 

The Ford Foundation partnered with Financial Health Network (FHN), a leading authority on financial health, to understand the feasibility of standing up a financial services organization, such as a credit union, specifically designed to serve people with disabilities. Research conducted by FHN found that the disability community faces numerous obstacles to financial inclusion, including banking services that fail to meet the needs of disabled people, high fees, limited access to low-cost credit, challenging asset limits, and low awareness in the financial sector of tools such as ABLE accounts. FHN’s research also found a lack of awareness of the diverse experiences and needs of people with disabilities and that most financial institutions are not courting the disability community as customers. 

Artichoke Credit Union is designed to help address these challenges through accessible banking, specialized financial education, responsible lending, inclusive product design, tools that support long-term financial well-being, and ongoing community-driven improvements. At launch, Artichoke Credit Union is expected to offer checking and savings accounts, certificates, personal loans, credit and debit cards, financial education resources, and budgeting tools. Members will also have access to support through live chat, phone, and video services, along with accessibility-focused features such as account alerts, guardian access options, and other custom-designed tools shaped by the needs of the community it serves.

MSUFCU is headquartered in East Lansing, Michigan, and has a long track record of building financial wellness for its members as a low-income designated credit union. A $5 membership share will establish membership with the credit union, and members will have access to support through live chat, phone, video services, and digital banking tools.

“The creation of Artichoke Credit Union is more than a new brand. It is an opportunity to listen, learn, and build alongside the disability community. Throughout our history, MSUFCU has embraced innovation to remove barriers and expand opportunity, from being among the first to offer accessible ATMs and supporting accessibility-focused lending programs to investing in innovative fintech solutions that create more inclusive experiences,” said April Clobes, president and CEO of MSUFCU. “As we serve more than 400,000 members, we remain committed to meeting each individual where they are and creating experiences that empower financial independence. We are proud to be the financial institution leading this initiative and further the credit union mission of making financial services more accessible, inclusive, and empowering for all.” 

The launch of Artichoke Credit Union is supported by two leaders of the disability rights movement: former senator Tom Harkin and former representative Tony Coelho, who were two of the primary Senate and House authors of the Americans With Disabilities Act (ADA). 

“In the 36 years since we passed the Americans With Disabilities Act, we have made tremendous progress when it comes to opening doors and breaking down physical barriers, but if a person with a disability cannot access the financial systems that fuel our economy, then the promise of full independence remains unfulfilled,” said Senator Tom Harkin. “True independence is not just about being able to physically get through the front door of a bank; it is about what you can do once you are inside, or when you log on to their app from home. When a banking website isn’t compatible with screen readers, or when a mobile payment app requires complex hand movements that are difficult to navigate, that is a modern-day barrier. That is exactly why a credit union dedicated to serving people with disabilities is so critically important. By providing accessible banking, fair lending, and financial literacy tailored to the community, Artichoke Credit Union is building an accessible digital workspace for people who just need a fair shot.”

“Economic justice for people with disabilities is part of the unfinished business of the ADA. For too long, issues like lack of accessibility and asset limits have restricted the potential for full economic inclusion and access to capital,” said Representative Tony Coelho. “Artichoke Credit Union addresses these challenges head-on by designing financial services in partnership with the disability community in order to serve a wide range of people with disabilities and their families. I am excited to support Artichoke Credit Union and look forward to becoming a proud member of the credit union when it launches next year.” 

Artichoke Credit Union is a trade name of MSUFCU, which is regulated by the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA). Deposits of up to $250,000 are federally insured.

Published in TIME

By Heather Gerken and Robert E. Rubin

Five years ago, in the wake of the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, America’s civic institutions pledged to do more to defend our system of fair and free elections. Major philanthropies increased their investments in programs that defend democracy. Law firms expanded their pro bono election-protection work. University presidents publicly condemned the effort to thwart the will of American voters. Many of the country’s largest businesses pledged to stop donating to candidates who had tried to overturn an election.

Today, our elections are again under attack. But while some institutions have maintained their commitment to defending democracy, far too many have retreated.

items.title: The Stakes of America’s 2026 Midterm Elections
items.summary:
• News and press
  • |In the press

Published in TIME

By Heather Gerken and Robert E. Rubin

Five years ago, in the wake of the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, America’s civic institutions pledged to do more to defend our system of fair and free elections. Major philanthropies increased their investments in programs that defend democracy. Law firms expanded their pro bono election-protection work. University presidents publicly condemned the effort to thwart the will of American voters. Many of the country’s largest businesses pledged to stop donating to candidates who had tried to overturn an election.

Today, our elections are again under attack. But while some institutions have maintained their commitment to defending democracy, far too many have retreated.

Throughout the performance, what initially appears to be a game gradually transforms into a surveillance system. Every gesture is recorded; every choice is absorbed; every mistake becomes part of the machine’s own logic. However, at a certain point, that logic breaks down—an unexpected presence alters the functioning of the space, fragmenting the language and turning the bodies into vehicles for a voice whose origin remains undefined.

Sound, light, fog, lasers, and movement interplay to create an environment of constant instability, where technology ceases to function merely as a theatrical tool and ultimately becomes an integral part of the experience. Blurring the lines between performance, installation, and sound composition, ‘AXIOM CASINO’ presents a space where the boundaries between control, perception, and transformation are in constant flux.

LISBON – With this project, DIVERGENTE developed tools to make the distribution of independent journalism more accessible and sustainable: a CRM to strengthen communication with institutions, local organisations and communities, and a dissemination hub where potential partners can discover DIVERGENTE’s live journalism formats, investigations and purpose. The tools supported outreach to underserved communities, including residents of disadvantaged neighbourhoods in Lisbon and rural areas, helping create new opportunities for them to engage directly with journalism and journalists.

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

Project Activities

With the funding, DIVERGENTE developed a set of tools and activities to strengthen the distribution of independent journalism and build more lasting relationships with underserved audiences.

The project’s main outputs were a CRM system and a dedicated dissemination hub for live journalism.

The CRM brought together and organised DIVERGENTE’s contacts, including local organisations, institutions, NGOs and community partners, allowing the newsroom to communicate more easily with specific communities and target outreach by location, interests and previous interactions.

The dissemination hub provides potential partners with a clear overview of what live journalism is, why it matters, which formats DIVERGENTE offers and which investigations can be brought to different communities. This makes it easier for organisations to understand the concept of live journalism and explore possible collaborations without relying on individual explanations.

The project also supported five live journalism activities in underserved territories. These events created opportunities for residents to meet journalists, engage with investigations and discuss the issues that matter to them. They also served to gather feedback through surveys, helping DIVERGENTE understand how participants relate to journalism, what information they find difficult to access and which topics they feel are missing from the media.

Together, these activities strengthened DIVERGENTE’s capacity to reach audiences beyond its existing networks and created the infrastructure needed to make community-based journalism more systematic, targeted and sustainable.

What is the impact?

The project contributed to addressing news deserts by strengthening DIVERGENTE’s capacity to reach communities that are underserved by existing media. It focused on creating the infrastructure needed for a longer-term response in media deserts: to communicate more systematically with relevant institutions and community organisations, facilitate partnerships around live journalism, and carry out pilot activities in underserved territories to collect feedback from communities to shape future action.

The impact on news deserts is therefore best understood as laying the foundations for a longer-term, scalable model of distribution and community engagement.

Through live journalism events in disadvantaged neighbourhoods, and suburbs of Lisbon as well as in rural areas, participants were able to watch and discuss investigations, ask questions and share their own perspectives. The activities also gave communities a space to express which topics they feel are missing from the media and what makes it difficult for them to access journalism.

The project also helped create relationships that went beyond individual events. In one of the live journalism events, for example, a group of youngsters who participated later visited DIVERGENTE’s newsroom and organised a collective interview with the team. While these are early signs rather than evidence of large-scale change, they show how bringing journalism closer to communities can create curiosity, participation and new forms of engagement with the media.

Project Links

  • Dissemination Hub, divergente.pt
  • Live Journalism Toolkit, divergente.pt

Project Pictures

Photos by Ricardo Venâncio Lopes

VELENJE - Empowerment Through Equity gave underrepresented people in Slovenia’s Šaleška and Koroška regions a stronger voice in local public debate. Through 36 radio programmes, 72 short segments, online stories and printed materials, Radio Velenje brought practical, accessible information to ethnic minorities, migrants and foreign residents, low-income families, young and older people, and others facing barriers to information and participation. 

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

The project also created lasting connections with individuals and community organisations that continue to enrich the station’s journalism.

By combining radio, digital publishing and face-to-face distribution through community partners, the project reached both digitally active audiences and people with limited online access. Listeners and organisations increasingly contacted the newsroom with questions, topic suggestions and stories, strengthening Radio Velenje’s role as a trusted and inclusive local platform.

Project Activities

With the funding, Radio Velenje implemented the following activities:

  • Produced and broadcast 36 weekly radio programmes featuring local stories, expert knowledge and lived experience related to inequality, inclusion, resilience and access to rights and services.
  • Produced and broadcast 72 short radio segments, aired twice per week, providing concise, practical and fact-based information.
  • Published project content online in the dedicated “Moč skozi pravičnost” section and promoted it through Radio Velenje’s social media channels.
  • Printed and distributed 2,000 flyers and 500 booklets through community organisations and local contact points, ensuring access for people with limited digital connectivity.
  • Actively involved women, young people, ethnic minorities, migrants and foreign residents, social workers, educators, community organisations and people with lived experience as guests, contributors and sources.

These activities broadened Radio Velenje’s source network, introduced new voices into its editorial output and strengthened direct dialogue with communities across the Šaleška and Koroška regions. Several new contacts later became contributors to regular programming beyond the funded activities, extending the project’s value for the outlet and its audiences.

What is the impact?

The project had a meaningful local impact in countering news deserts because it expanded the range of public-interest information and perspectives available in the Šaleška and Koroška regions. It gave sustained editorial space to people and issues that are often overlooked in mainstream or highly centralised coverage, including the experiences of minorities, migrants and foreign residents, low-income families, young people, older people and community organisations. Regular radio programmes, short segments, online articles and printed materials ensured that this information was not limited to a single platform or to audiences with reliable digital access.

The project also strengthened the local information ecosystem itself. More individuals and organisations approached Radio Velenje with stories, questions and proposals for future coverage, helping the newsroom identify issues that might otherwise remain invisible. The resulting network of sources and contributors continues beyond the grant period, improving the outlet’s capacity to provide inclusive, locally rooted journalism and sustain media plurality in the region.

The clearest positive change was greater visibility and participation for people who are often underrepresented in local media. Community members increasingly contacted the newsroom, proposed topics, asked to present their work and shared personal experiences. This showed that audiences did not only receive information; they also recognised Radio Velenje as an open and trusted place where their concerns and perspectives could be heard.
