Lorenzo Di Stasi is an independent Italian journalist based in Brussels.

James Jackson

James Jackson is a freelance investigative reporter and broadcaster based in Berlin.

Stefano Valentino is a Brussels-based freelance investigative journalist.

Related projects

    Driving Deforestation. European Luxury Cars' Impact on Indigenous Lands

    ASUNCIÓN - The investigation reveals the links between the European car industry and massive deforestation in Paraguay's Chaco region. It reveals how major luxury car brands such as BMW and Mercedes-Benz buy leather from Italian companies, which in turn source the material from Paraguayan companies involved in illegal deforestation, particularly in the Ayoreo indigenous territories.

    Meer lezen
  • © Marta Abbà

    TIRANA/MILANO - The destruction of the Balkans' forests continues, especially in the remote areas of Albania where the law doesn't reach and corruption reigns. It's a deep-rooted and local phenomenon, but it's supported by an international dynamic that involves Europe and, above all, the country's best partner in crime: Italy.

    Meer lezen

    JAKARTA – This investigation reveals serious irregularities and testimonies of environmental and social fraud at the Weda Bay Nickel, the world's largest open pit nickel mine, co-owned by the French mining giant Eramet, the Chinese steel multinational Tsinghan and the Indonesian state through the state-owned company PT Antam.

The investigation explicitly distinguishes between documented supply-chain links and physical traceability: no material evidence conclusively proves that nickel from these two mines was incorporated into a specific CATL battery cell shipped to Volkswagen. Companies and relevant authorities were approached for comment, and their responses or refusals to provide details were incorporated into the reporting.

OSTRAVA – To address the lack of in-depth regional coverage in the Moravian-Silesian Region, Okraj.cz launched the Local Lens project to cultivate a new generation of local journalists. Through an intensive mentoring programme, three young reporters published investigative features on overlooked national minorities, produced podcasts, and hosted public discussions. 

On this page

  • Activities
  • Impact
  • Links
  • Photos

The initiative directly enriched the local information ecosystem, giving a platform to underrepresented communities while strengthening the publication's long-term capacity to cover regional news deserts.

Project Activities

Between September 2025 and May 2026, Okraj.cz implemented a comprehensive capacity-building initiative for three selected journalism interns: Barbora, Vojtěch, and Natálie. Paired with personal mentors, the interns participated in an intensive editorial bootcamp in Krnov, featuring tailored workshops on local ethics and in-depth reporting, as well as an expert session on local media environments led by Masaryk University academic Lenka Waschková Císařová.

Throughout the programme, the interns engaged in multi-format reporting, ranging from quick-response news for the "Week in the Region" format to covering local municipal council meetings. The core of their work focused on producing three major long-form investigative features on ethnic minorities in the region, exploring Greek identity, Polish cross-border healthcare dynamics, and German cultural heritage in Hlučínsko. Enhanced by professional photography by Kateřina Šimečková and illustrations by Tereza Ignácová, the project also produced dedicated podcast episodes and culminated in May 2026 with a public panel discussion titled "Moravian-Silesia Among Nations."

What is the impact?

The Local Lens project directly tackled the phenomenon of regional news deserts by injecting fresh, professional editorial resources into the Moravian-Silesian Region. By training and mentoring early-career journalists, the initiative built sustainable local media capacity rather than providing a temporary patch. The long-term impact is evidenced by two of the three interns transitioning into permanent editorial positions at Okraj.cz, ensuring that the region retains skilled reporters dedicated to scrutinising local government and covering underserved topics. Furthermore, the systematic framework created during the PM4D grant period served as a model that successfully attracted follow-up funding from the Endowment Fund for Independent Journalism (NFNŽ) and the Daniel Anýž Fund, securing the newsroom's ongoing presence in the area.

The project brought significantly greater visibility to historically marginalised or overlooked communities within the region, specifically the local Greek, Polish, and German minorities. By moving beyond surface-level reporting to explore complex topics like cross-border healthcare and regional identity, Okraj.cz provided its readership with nuanced, contextual local journalism. Beyond written coverage, the project fostered direct civic engagement through its public panel discussion, "Moravian-Silesia Among Nations," creating a physical space for dialogue between community members, journalists, and local stakeholders.

This call for proposals supports publishers in the publication of original works of cultural and scientific interest in Portuguese, or the translation of key works.

The objectives of the support are:

  • To encourage the circulation of works that reflect original and innovative thinking in the fields of the Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences, as well as high-quality translation;
  • To encourage publishers’ activity and contribution to an open and inclusive cultural debate;
  • To contribute to the revitalisation of the book market in publishing areas that are less commercially viable.

Conditions

Original and unpublished works of cultural, artistic, scientific or philosophical interest may be submitted in the following fields:

  • Arts (non-fiction);
  • Humanities (non-fiction;
  • Social Sciences (non-fiction);
  • Translation (literature or non-fiction).

Funding will be awarded for one or more of the following stages of book production (print or digital):

  • Copyrights;
  • Proofreading;
  • Translation;
  • Graphic design;
  • Layout;
  • Printing;
  • Finishing.

Funding may cover up to 100% of the total project budget, up to a maximum amount of €10,000.

The results will be announced online by 15 January 2027.

Eligibility

  • Private legal entities, such as commercial companies, cooperatives or associations, whose main corporate purpose and articles of association relate to the editing and publication of books, are eligible to apply for funding (applicant organisations must have been in continuous operation for at least two years);

  • The books must be published within 18 months of the grant being awarded;

  • Each publisher may submit only one application per year;

  • Only online applications in Portuguese will be accepted.

How to Apply

  • Register to apply;

  • Before submitting your application form, please check all the eligibility requirements. We recommend that you read the Call Conditions (available in the Documents section) and the Frequently Asked Questions (in Portuguese);

  • The application will only be accepted once all the mandatory fields on the form have been completed and the documentation required in the Call Conditions has been uploaded;

  • Finally, click on the ‘Submit application’ button. To avoid any issues when submitting your application, please do not wait until the last few days of the deadline to submit it.

Contacts

If you still have any questions after reading the FAQs and the rules, please contact the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation via [email protected]

• Gulbenkian Orchestra

    In 1962, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation decided to establish a permanent orchestral ensemble. Originally with only twelve musicians (strings and continuo) it was named “Orquestra de Câmara Gulbenkian”. This collective was successively enlarged and today the “Orquestra Gulbenkian” (the name it has adopted since 1971) has a permanent body of sixty instrumentalists, a number that can be expanded depending on the repertoire.

    This structure allows the Gulbenkian Orchestra to interpret works from the Baroque and Classical periods, a significant part of 19th century orchestral literature and much of the music of the 20th century, including works belonging to the current repertoire of the traditional symphonic orchestras. In each season, the orchestra performs on a regular series of concerts at the Gulbenkian Grand Auditorium in Lisbon, where it has had the opportunity of working together with some of leading names of the world of music (conductors and soloists). It has also performed on numerous locations all over Portugal, in an effort to decentralize music and culture.

    The orchestra has been constantly expanding its activities in the international level, performing in Europe, Asia Africa, and the Americas. In the recording field, Orquestra Gulbenkian is associated to labels as Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Hyperion, Teldec, Erato, Adès, Nimbus, Lyrinx, Naïve and Pentatone, among others, and this activity was recognized with several international prizes.

    Hannu Lintu is the Music Director of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2023.

  • Paweł Kapuła

    Conductor

    Paweł Kapuła, hailed by Polish Radio as “a real hope for Polish conducting” is one of the most spectacular and finest conductors of the younger generation, acclaimed for his exciting, fresh, and highly captivating interpretations coupled with an excellent conducting technique. Never afraid of a challenge, his programmes and conducting style demonstrate a high level of finesse and creativity, which has led to an ever-growing presence in Europe and beyond.

    The 2024/25 season sees Paweł Kapuła debut with some of the world’s leading orchestras, amongst them Japan Philharmonic Orchestra, Xi’an Symphony Orchestra and Guiyang Symphony Orchestra alongside Hamburger Symphoniker, Danish Chamber Orchestra and Robert-Schumann-Philharmonie Chemnitz. He will also return to Ulster Orchestra where he received a prompt re-invitation following his highly successful debut last season. Other guest engagements include the Georgian Chamber Orchestra and Württembergische Philharmonie Reutlingen, which have now grown into loyal partners cherishing him for his vigorous persona and precise conducting style.

    Previously, Paweł Kapuła made his debut with orchestras such as Oslo Opera Orchestra and Aarhus Symphony Orchestra, resulting in immediate re-invitations, Sibiu Philharmonic and Transylvanian State Philharmonic orchestras in Romania, Gothenburg Opera Orchestra, Sinfonieorchester Basel and Südwestdeutsche Philharmonie Konstanz.

    In February 2021, Paweł Kapuła was appointed Principal Guest Conductor of Pomeranian Philharmonic in Bydgoszcz. Since then, he has been leading the orchestra in programmes with such refinement and flair that it has attracted other Polish orchestras’ attention, amongst them Polish National Radio Symphony Orchestra Katowice, Warsaw Philharmonic and Baltic Philharmonic Gdańsk.

    His latest recording project of all the Beethoven Piano Concertos with Prague Philharmonic Orchestra at Prague’s Rudolfinum, has just seen its international release. Paweł Kapuła is also an avid champion of neglected Polish composers which he demonstrates in numerous recordings for Polish Radio.

    Paweł Kapuła received his first piano lessons at the age of seven. He studied conducting with Tadeusz Strugala and Stanislaw Krawczynski at Krakow’s Academy of Music. He was a finalist and winner of the Distinction Award at the first Adam Kopyciński Student Conducting Competition in Wroclaw in 2013 and is a musicology graduate of the Jagiellonian University in Krakow.

EU - Despite EU water laws, this summer the drinking water supply system showed serious cracks in several regions in the European Union. Good water governance and its enforcement are essential to safeguard the access to clean drinking water on our continent. The European Commission is stepping up its efforts to safeguard access to clean and healthy drinking water in the near future, but the road ahead will be winding.

How can persistent drinking water problems remain while new ones are popping up everywhere in Europe, when appropriate European water laws are in place? After investigating real-life situations in several European Member States, the answers are obvious. There is a lack of good water governance, trustworthy data and adequate enforcement, and the sector is facing a serious investment gap. All these things can be addressed, but this needs to be done quickly, because reversing these kind of developments will be hard, if not impossible.

Key Findings

The team of journalists investigated five cases in different Member States, and the results are sometimes quite shocking. In Spain drinking water pollution by livestock farms is a big problem. It leaves many villages without safe and healthy drinking water. In Abruzzo more than half of its water is lost through old, never-replaced networks, while some areas go without water for days. “I shower down at the sea, because I know at home I can’t”, says one on the inhabitants.

In a water-rich country such as The Netherlands the drinking water supply system needs to change drastically. The national government needs to take the lead and start changing national laws to safeguard drinking water in the near future. In Sweden tensions are running high about drinking water prices due to the country’s aging water treatment infrastructure. In Ireland the drinking water supply of the city of Dublin is at stake due to failing infrastructure.

Methodology

The cross-border investigation combined desk research, field reporting and interviews across the countries examined. The journalists conducted interviews in person, online and by email and visited selected regions to document local water challenges and infrastructure.

The team also held regular cross-border meetings to compare findings, identify common patterns and develop new reporting angles.

Water-law expert Marleen van Rijswick provided legal guidance throughout the investigation and reviewed the articles to assess their interpretation of relevant European and national water legislation.

Themes

  • Environment
  • Healthcare

Publication

ONLINE

  • Nelle falle del sistema: il paradosso di una terra ricca d’acqua, Prismag, 01/10/2026
  • Vattnets pris behöver räknas om, Cirkulation, 01/10/2026
  • Wetswijzigingen nodig om Nederlands drinkwater veilig te stellen, H2O Water Network, 08/10/2026

More to come

Esther Rasenberg is a Dutch freelance journalist and communications advisor.

Cecilia Fasciani is an Italian freelance journalist and documentary filmmaker.

Else Beekman is an independent Dutch journalist based in Spain.

Joakim Rådström is an independent Swedish journalist.

Related projects

    The Hidden Threat: Asbestos Fibres in Our Drinking Water

    BRUSSELS – Asbestos is now banned in 69 countries, but it is still found in our drinking water. Water pipes are made of asbestos cement release fibres that can be lethal when inhaled. Experts have warned about this problem for decades, but the issue persists. 

    Meer lezen
  • cc

    The Silent Threat of Untreated Wastewater

    TBILISI / YEREVAN / ODESA / KHERSON –  The Silent Threat of Untreated Wastewater investigates the growing public health and environmental crisis caused by untreated wastewater in Armenia, Georgia, and Ukraine.

    Meer lezen

  • PFAS in Belgian spring water

    BRUSSELS - Spring and mineral waters from the Ardennes, the High Fens and East Flanders contain traces of ultra short PFAS. Analyses ordered by Apache show that TFA has seeped deep into the natural water veins.

Fellows are encouraged to pursue projects of their own choosing in a setting designed to encourage reflection, concentration, and exchange. Bringing together scholars from a wide range of disciplines, backgrounds, and nationalities, the program seeks to create a vibrant intellectual community while supporting individual research of outstanding quality and originality.

Applications will be assessed through a competitive international process. The quality and originality of the proposed work, in keeping with the Institute’s spirit and intellectual environment, will be central considerations in the evaluation of candidates. The final cohort will be selected by the GIAS Advisory Board.

Eligibility

The GIAS will host international academics, but will also consider applications from emeriti, independent scholars, and artists. Applications in most non-laboratorial and non-experimental fields will be considered, provided that the proposed work is not primarily practice- or application-oriented.

How to Apply

Applicants to the fellowships should submit their applications individually, and include a curriculum vitae, a brief description of what they propose to do while at the GIAS, and the names of two referees. 

Fellowship offers will be made from late January of the following year.

Visual and Sound Artist Residencies facilitate mobility and artistic exchanges of V4 citizens in the fields of visual and sound arts, including design, music, video and film, new media and mixed media.

At-a-Glance Criteria

  • Eligibility & Scope: Applicants V4 citizens age 18+; the residency must take place in a V4 country other than the applicant’s country of citizenship/residence.
  • Duration & timing: Lasting 2 months between January 10 and December 31
  • Funding: €6,000 total per project — €3,000 for the resident and €3,000 for the host organization

Guidelines & Files

Timeline

Sep 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Call opens

Oct 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Final application deadline

Dec 20, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Results announced

Jan 10, 2027 at 12:00 PM: Project start

Visual and Sound Artist Residencies are open to artists working in the following disciplines: Visual Arts (including performance art, textile art and architecture), Design (fashion, costume, jewelry, ceramics and furniture design, visual communication), Music/Sound (interpretation, sound installation, sound performance, composition) and Video/Film/New Media/Mixed Media (including video installation).

  • The residency must be implemented in a V4 country, other than that of the applicant’s citizenship/residence
  • The period of support is 2 months
  • Residencies can take place between January 10 to December 31
  • Reapplying of previously supported artists is possible only for a residency in a V4 country different that of the previous residency project
  • The amount of the support is €3,000 for resident and €3,000 for the host organization for the two months of the residency; each res­i­dency project receives €6,000 in total.

The Final Report in the form of a questionnaire is  to be submitted by the artist and the host institution no later than 30 days after the end of the residency. To ensure the timely disbursement of the final installment, residents are kindly requested to complete the questionnaire within 30 days after the conclusion of their residency. The questionnaire is completed in the My Visegrad system.

Additionally, residents are required to upload images captured during their residency and provide web links to any related posts. 

The host organization is responsible for completing, printing, and signing a separate questionnaire. Following this, residents are kindly requested to upload the completed questionnaire from the host organization (pdf file) as part of their Final Report through My Visegrad system and submit the entire report.

Technical problems with online application and other questions should be addressed to Project Manager Martin Marciňa.

The application form must be submitted via My Visegrad by October 15 at 12.00 PM (noon). The online application system opens at noon on September 15.

Your application must include the following enclosures:

  • Copy of your ID or passport
  • Artistic portfolio  (file or link to artist's website)
  • The applicant chooses the host organization and submits a preliminary confirmation of acceptance

Explore more

Check our Frequently Asked Questions for answers about this opportunity.

Visual Artist Residency in New York provides artists with the chance to be inspired in a variety of spectacular artistic settings of Brooklyn. Every year, four artists get the incredible opportunity to engage with peers and focus on process and experimentation. The program gives artists complete freedom during their residency, but also provides resources and weekly lectures for guidance and feedback.

At-a-Glance Criteria

  • Eligibility: Visual artists from V4 countries, with good spoken and written English.
  • Residency: Lasting 2 months from July 1 until August 31
  • Funding: for each artist €7,000 to cover accommodation, travel, subsistence, and necessary materials.

Guidelines & Files

Timeline

Sep 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Call opens

Oct 15, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Final application deadline

Dec 20, 2026 at 12:00 PM: Results announced

Jul 1, 2027 at 12:00 PM: Project start

The residency program at International Studio & Curatorial Program in New York, USA creates an environment for inspiration, dialogue, and experimentation. It allows four artists (one from each Visegrad country) to experience life and work in a unique community where creativity is applied to the everyday and offers conditions that enrich the creativity.

ISCP was founded in 1994 with the mission to support and enhance the professional development of emerging to mid-career artists and curators from around the world, introduce New York audiences to exceptional international art practices and engage the communities of Brooklyn and the New York City area through public programs that enrich the appreciation and understanding of contemporary art.

The program is suited to visual artists, artists with interdisciplinary practices.

  • Applicants are visual artists from V4 countries, only a single artist per V4 country annually
  • Good knowledge of English both spoken and written
  • Applicants have not received art scholarships in New York in the past (preference)
  • The residency period is 2 months, July 1 to August 31
  • The amount of support for each artist is €7,000 to cover accommodation, travel costs, subsistence during the stay, as well as purchasing of materials necessary for the respective artistic activity

For more information about general conditions and selection criteria, read the Rules of the Visegrad Artists Residency Program

Technical problems with online application should be addressed to Project Manager Martin Marciňa.

The application form must be submitted via My Visegrad by October 15 at 12.00 PM (noon). The online application system opens on September 15.

Your application must include the following enclosures:

  • Copy of your ID or passport
  • Your CV and motivation letter (including your project plan)
  • Artistic portfolio (file or link to artist´s website)

Applicants are selected on the basis of their previous work, their potential contribution to the residency stay in New York, as well as the potential benefit they can draw from the program. Only one artist per V4 country is supported annually.

Explore more

items.content_html:
CROATIA / ITALY - This investigation looks at how beaches in Italy and Croatia continue to receive the prestigious Blue Flag certification despite persistent failures to comply with EU wastewater treatment standards.

Every summer, the Blue Flag tells beachgoers that a beach meets strict environmental standards, and one of the scheme’s criteria is that urban wastewater is properly treated. Yet Italy is among the worst performers in the European Union under the Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive. The EU Court of Justice has condemned it repeatedly, and it paid more than €210 million in penalties by the end of 2024. Croatia, on the other side of the Adriatic, is also still far from compliance. The Dirty Adriatic asks how the two are able to coexist: how can a certification that guarantees clean water be awarded along coastlines where the public record says wastewater is not properly collected or treated?

The investigation compares official record systems that normally never meet. These are the countries’ own reporting to the European Union on wastewater collection and treatment, the Blue Flag lists and awarding rules, rulings by the EU Court of Justice, and independent bathing-water sampling. It then follows the money and the paperwork behind the certification: who pays for it, with which public funds, and which documents municipalities submit to obtain it. The story comes at a turning point. From 27 September 2026, EU Directive 2024/825 on green claims tightens the rules on sustainability labels and environmental claims presented to consumers.

Methodologically, the team rebuilt Italy’s national submissions under the directive across several reporting cycles and linked them spatially to Blue Flag sites. The findings show inconsistencies and overlaps between official sources, not causal claims. They are backed by around twenty freedom-of-information requests to municipalities, regions, and environmental agencies, municipal administrative records, and field reporting on the Italian and Croatian coasts.

Themes

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

  • Spiagge Bandiere Blu, il mistero delle procedure e le anomalie nella selezione dei luoghi, Domani, 12/10/2026

Team members

Sebastian Viskanic

Sebastian Viskanic is a creative media professional, journalist and filmmaker based in Rome.

Jelena Prtorić

Jelena Prtorić is a Croatian freelance journalist based in Berlin.

Filippo Poltronieri

Filippo Poltronieri is a journalist and videomaker based in Rome.

Related projects

  • © Christina Anna Orieschnig

    Varna's Hazardous Seafood Exports Throughout Europe

    VARNA - Improper management of a wastewater treatment pipe in the Varna lake has led to repeated toxic leaks since 2019. 

    Meer lezen

  • The Disappearance of Prespa Lake

    PRESPA LAKE – Prespa lake in North Macedonia is considered even older than the "official" oldest lake in Europe, Ohrid Lake. And it is under threat.

    Meer lezen

  • Dirty Money for Clean Rivers

    BUCHAREST - For almost 9 years, Romania has been criticised and monitored by the European Commission for allowing the large-scale destruction of several mountain rivers for the purpose of building micro-hydropower plants, without complying with the Water Framework and Habitats Directives.

    Meer lezen

MILAN / WARSAW / KYIV - How Europe's exceptional welcome of 2022 turned into years of permanent uncertainty, exposing the cracks of a reception system that expects people in need to accept whatever they are offered.

The arrival of millions of Ukrainians in 2022 is remembered as a unique act of European solidarity, and it was one. For the first time, temporary protection was activated, and people fleeing the war received legal status, the right to work, healthcare and freedom of movement almost overnight. In Italy, around 170,000 people found shelter, mostly in the homes of relatives, the long-established Ukrainian community and Italian families who opened their doors within days. In Poland, a country more used to sending people abroad than receiving them, an emergency law gave refugees equal access to healthcare and child benefits, and civil society took in hundreds of thousands of people.

This story also has a darker side. More than four years later, the emergency has not ended, and protection that was meant to be temporary has become a permanent state of uncertainty. Permits are still renewed one year at a time, now up to March 2028. Every extension or legal change arrives late and unpredictably, and none of these years count towards a lasting status. Many refugees, for their part, still live with a suspended migration project. They did not choose to leave, they see their stay as a pause, and they put off learning the language or planning a future, because giving up on return feels like a surrender.

Key Findings

  • Prolonged temporariness has shown what happens when a status built for a short emergency is stretched over years. Every renewal puts access to healthcare, family benefits and housing at risk, and every announced legal change sends people rushing to offices to secure their rights. Bureaucracy creates closed circles. Without a registered address there is no ID, without ID there is no bank account, and without a bank account a person with a job cannot be paid. Welfare and social housing schemes require permits or years of residence that a one-year status can never provide. The new routes to longer-term permits reward those with stable contracts and leave the elderly, carers and single mothers behind. As collective accommodation closes, some people fall into homelessness, including men sent back from other EU countries.
  • The assumption that people who arrive in need, and who are foreigners, should accept whatever they are offered. The investigation found it at every step. Many people end up in informal sublets, and some are asked by agents for upfront fees. Landlords demand deposits worth several months of rent, hang up when they hear a foreign accent, or blame a whole nationality for one tenant's damage. Doctors, engineers and pharmacists clean houses because recognising a diploma is costly and slow. Some employers expect gratitude and silence instead of fair pay. Those who ask questions or claim their rights are quickly labelled demanding. The Ukrainian experience makes visible a mindset that weighs on everyone who depends on the reception system.
  • Scattered across both countries, there are also examples of good integration. They tend to appear where the local community plays an active part and where a Ukrainian community was already present: parishes, local associations, Caritas networks, diaspora organisations and families who stayed by people's side for years. Most households have at least one member in regular work, and many have rebuilt a fragile stability. These successes, however, depend on goodwill rather than on the system. Volunteer support faded within one or two years, public attention dropped, and in both countries political tensions, sensationalist media and disinformation eroded the early solidarity. The system keeps confirming and perpetuating the mechanisms that weigh on refugees' future and on their mental health. Living from one deadline to the next creates constant anxiety. People cannot plan six months ahead, and many spend years in reception facilities, losing hope without gaining a plan. Families are split by conscription rules, and some parents have not seen their children for years. Many grieve the professional identity they built at home. Everyday hostility, online attacks and a silence that keeps most victims from reporting abuse add fear to uncertainty.

Methodology

The project brings together a team working in Italy, Poland and Ukraine and uses the same method in both host countries. For more than six months, the team conducted in-depth interviews with researchers, reception coordinators, social workers, cultural mediators, housing specialists, civic activists and psychologists, and gathered personal testimonies separately from refugees of different ages and backgrounds. In Italy, fieldwork covered Lombardy, Veneto and Trentino. In Poland, interviews were combined with a mystery-call investigation of the rental market in six cities. The research was also enriched by a conversation with project advisor Nellija Locmele, who provided an additional perspective on the issues explored. Interviews with Ukrainian and European experts on migration policy, return prospects and integration indicators frame both national cases.

  • Armed conflict
  • Migration
  • Social affairs

Those who ask questions or claim their rights are quickly labelled demanding. The Ukrainian experience makes visible a mindset that weighs on everyone who depends on the reception system.
  • Scattered across both countries, there are also examples of good integration. They tend to appear where the local community plays an active part and where a Ukrainian community was already present: parishes, local associations, Caritas networks, diaspora organisations and families who stayed by people's side for years. Most households have at least one member in regular work, and many have rebuilt a fragile stability. These successes, however, depend on goodwill rather than on the system. Volunteer support faded within one or two years, public attention dropped, and in both countries political tensions, sensationalist media and disinformation eroded the early solidarity. The system keeps confirming and perpetuating the mechanisms that weigh on refugees' future and on their mental health. Living from one deadline to the next creates constant anxiety. People cannot plan six months ahead, and many spend years in reception facilities, losing hope without gaining a plan. Families are split by conscription rules, and some parents have not seen their children for years. Many grieve the professional identity they built at home. Everyday hostility, online attacks and a silence that keeps most victims from reporting abuse add fear to uncertainty.

Methodology

The project brings together a team working in Italy, Poland and Ukraine and uses the same method in both host countries. For more than six months, the team conducted in-depth interviews with researchers, reception coordinators, social workers, cultural mediators, housing specialists, civic activists and psychologists, and gathered personal testimonies separately from refugees of different ages and backgrounds. In Italy, fieldwork covered Lombardy, Veneto and Trentino. In Poland, interviews were combined with a mystery-call investigation of the rental market in six cities. The research was also enriched by a conversation with project advisor Nellija Locmele, who provided an additional perspective on the issues explored. Interviews with Ukrainian and European experts on migration policy, return prospects and integration indicators frame both national cases.

Date

  • 17:30 / Cancelled 17:30 / Sold out Monday, 17:30

Location

Pricing

Through the beauty of Portugal’s landscapes and the accounts of those working on the ground or contributing to this collective effort, we discover projects dedicated to protecting habitats and species. We also see how associations, local authorities, schools and communities work together towards shared goals.

Beyond showing the work carried out in the field, Guardians of Natural Heritage invites us to reflect on how we care for the land and the role each of us can play in building a more sustainable future.

Before the screening, Daniel Espírito Santo, the documentary’s director, will briefly introduce the film and describe the process behind it, from the initial idea through to the finished film.

The screening will be followed by a discussion with Daniel Espírito Santo, the documentary’s director; Estrela Matilde, a biologist and Executive Director of LPN – Liga para a Proteção da Natureza; and Manuel Malva, a biologist and Vice-President of Milvoz – Associação de Proteção e Conservação da Natureza. The discussion will be moderated by Sofia Barbeiro, a project manager at the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation.

Drawing on the experience of those working in the field, the discussion will explore some of the issues raised by the film, including current challenges for nature conservation in Portugal.

Guardians of Our Natural Heritage will be presented at a preview screening in Portugal before being shown in Yerevan, Armenia, during Biodiversity COP17.

The eight environmental organisations featured in the film are supported by the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation through its core funding programme.

items.content_html:
• Telmo Costa

    Clarinet

    Telmo began his musical studies when he was 7 years old with José Américo Belinha in Tuna Musical de São Paio de Oleiros. Then, he started studying with Hélder Tavares in Academia de Música de Paços de Brandão, where he finished highschool with distinction. He attended several masterclasses with António Saiote, Nuno Pinto, Florent Héau, François Benda, Kilian Herold, Harri Mäki, among others.

    He was awarded with many prizes in national and international competitions, such as 1st Prize in “Concurso Luso-espanhol” (Fafe), 1st Prize in International Clarinet Competition APC, Golden Prize in Vienna International Music Competition, 1st Prize in North International Music Competition and 1st Prize in “Prémio Jovens Músicos”. In this very competition, he was awarded with three more prizes, the Young Musician of the Year (“Maestro Silva Pereira Prize”), European Union of Music Competitions for Youth Prize, and “Prémio Círculo Richard Wagner”.

    As far as his orchestral experience is concerned, he took part in Jovem Orquestra Portuguesa (2013-2017), Estágio Gulbenkian para Orquestra (2017 and 2018), Gustav Mahler Jugendorchester (2016 and 2018), Neue Philhamornie München (2018) and Schweizer Jugendsinfonieorchester (2018). He also collaborated with Orquestra Filarmónica Portuguesa, Luzerner Sinfonieorchester and Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra. In 2019 he won the academy position in Luzerner Sinfonieorchester and 1st Soloist co-principal in Orquestra Gulbenkian. He is currently studying in Hochschule für Musik Basel in Switzerland with François Benda.

  • Pedro Fernandes

    French Horn

    Pedro Miguel Pereira Fernandes was born in 1990 in Viana do Castelo. He initially studied at the Escola Profissional de Música de Viana do Castelo under the teachers Sónia Feijó and Bruno Rafael. In 2008, he was admitted to the Escola Superior de Música e Artes do Espetáculo do Porto (ESMAE) where he studied with Bohdan Sebestik and Abel Pereira and graduated in 2012. In 2017, he completed his master’s degree in Education at the University of Minho’s Instituto de Educação.

    He has taken part in and attended masterclasses in Portugal and abroad given by Ab Koster, Abel Pereira, Froydis Ree Wekre, Hermann Baumann, Javier Bonet, Jindřich Petrás, Jiří Havlik, Jonathan Luxton, José Bernardo Silva, Michelle Stebleton, Radovan Vlatkovic, Spanish Brass Luur Metalls, Will Sanders, Zdeněk Divoký and Zoltán Mácsai, among others.

    In 2008, he came second in the youth category at the 1st “Terras de La Salette” National Wind Instrument Competition and in 2019 he was awarded first place in the senior category, as well as the Dona Aldina Prize, at the 14th “Terras de La Salette” International Wind Instrument Competition.

    He has been a member of the Orquestra APROARTE, Orquesta Joven de la Sinfónica de Galicia, Gustav Mahler Jugendorchester and Banda Sinfónica Portuguesa. As a guest performer, he has played with the Orquestra Sinfónica do Porto Casa da Música, Orquestra de Câmara do Minho, Orquestra Metropolitana de Lisboa, Gulbenkian Orchestra, Fundação Orquestra Estúdio, Orquesta de la Comunidade de Madrid, Orquestra Clássica da Madeira, Oviedo Filarmonía, BBC Philharmonic, BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra, Remix Ensemble Casa da Música, Orquestra Sinfónica de Bilbau and Orquesta Sinfónica del Principado de Asturias directed by renowned conductors such as Antoni Rós Marbá, Antonio Pappano, Christoph König, Daniele Gatti, David Afkham, Douglas Bostock, Eliahu Inbal, Emilio Pomàrico, Evgeny Bushkov, Gilbert Varga, Harry Lith, Herbert Blomstedt, James Judd, John Storgårds, Jonathan Nott, Joseph Vicente, Joseph Young, Juanjo Mena, Kent Nagano, Kirill Petrenko, Leo Mcfall, Lothar Zagrosek, Michael Sanderling, Michael Zilm, Olari Elts, Peter Rundel, Pietro Rizzo, Philippe Jordan, Simone Young, Sir Colin Davis, Takuo Yuasa and Yoel Gamzou. He is currently a member of the Gulbenkian Orchestra and the Quarteto Português de Trompas.

  • Ricardo Ramos

    Bassoon

    Ricardo Ramos began his musical training at the ARTAVE School in 1997. He continued his studies at the Escola Superior de Música e Artes do Espetáculo do Porto, under Hugues Kesteman. He also studied at Musikhochschule Lübeck, in Germany, with Pierre Martens. He was a member of several youth and professional orchestras: Orquestra Portuguesa das Escolas de Música, Gustav Mahler Jugendorchester, European Youth Orchestra, Bamberg Symphony Orchestra, Hansestadt Lübeck Philharmonic Orchestra, Orquestra Nacional do Porto, REMIX Orquestra, Orquestra das Beiras and Orquestra do Norte. He has played under the baton of such important masters as Herbert Blomstedt, Esa-Pekka Salonen, Kirill Petrenko, Michael Boder, Lawrence Foster, Michel Corboz, Ton Koopman and Bertrand de Billy, among others

    As a soloist, he has played with the Kiel Philharmonic Orchestra, the Gulbenkian Orchestra, the Orquestra da Escola Superior de Música e Artes do Espetáculo and the Norddeutsche Sinfonietta.

    He won the Estoril Competition (2011) and the RDP Young Musicians Prize (2003 and 2008), the Helena Sá e Costa Competition (2005), the Possehl Wettbewerb Music Prize (2008) and the Porto Rotary Club Competition (2007). A prize from the Solti Foundation enabled him to participate in several events organised by the foundation in England.

    Ricardo Ramos is a bassoon teacher on the Music Degree Programme at the Piaget Institute/ISEIT, in Almada. He has been leader of the bassoon section of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2009.

  • Maria Balbi

    Violin

    Maria Balbi was born into a family of musicians, in Lima, Peru. She began piano lessons at the age of three and violin at five. She attended the National Conservatory of Lyon in France, where she graduated with the Gold Medal in Violin. She later studied at the National Conservatory of Music in Paris with Jacques Ghestem, Alain Meunier and Christian Ivaldi, receiving first prizes in violin and chamber music. Afterwards she studied with Phillip Hirshorn and Viktor Liberman at the Hochschule von dem Kunsten in Utrecht, the Netherlands, and with Tibor Varga at the École des Archets in Sion, Switzerland.

    As a soloist, she has played with the Orchestre d'Aubagne on a tour in France and with the Gulbenkian Orchestra in Lisbon. She regularly performs in Europe, Asia and the United States, including music festivals, where she has played with the Amsterdam Chamber Music Ensemble, the Moscow Piano Quartet and the Gulbenkian Orchestra Soloists.

    In addition to her activities as a classical violinist, Maria Balbi founded the fado group Trinados, with which she toured in Portugal, Morocco, Spain, Brazil and the United States of America. She is a member of the Moscow Piano Quartet and first violin of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 1999.

  • Maria José Laginha

    Violin

    Maria José Laginha was born in Lisbon. She studied at the Fundação Musical dos Amigos das Crianças and the Escola Profissional Artística do Vale do Ave (Artave) with Filomena Cardoso, Leonor Prado, Alberto Gaio Lima and Suzanne Lidegran. With a scholarship from Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation, she completed her studies with Aníbal Lima at the Academia Nacional Superior de Orquestra. She won the Prémio Jovens Músicos in 2005. She has attended masterclasses by Christoph Schikedanz (Kissingen Sommer), Roman Nodel, Igor Oistrakh, Igor Volochine, Chistophe Poiget (Rencontres Musicales en Lorraine), Boris Kuniev, Daniel Rowland (Stift International Music Festival), Richard Gwilt (Baroque violin), Alexei Mijlin and Felix Andrievsky.

    During her formative years, she joined several youth orchestras, such as the European Union Youth Orchestra and the World Orchestra, and toured worldwide. She also played with the Orquestra Aproarte, Sinfonietta de Lisboa, Lisbon Chamber Orchestra, Orquestra Metropolitana de Lisboa and Orquestra de Câmara Portuguesa and played solo with the Orquestra Artave, the Filarmonia da Beiras and the Gulbenkian Orchestra. She has been a member of the Camerata Atlântica since its creation in 2013. She was a teacher with the Orquestra Geração. She has been a member of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2007.

  • Samuel Barsegian

    Viola

    A native of Armenia, Samuel Barsegian began studying violin at the age of six at the Tchaikovsky Special School of Music, but at the age of fifteen he decided to switch to the viola. He graduated in 1989 and then pursued his studies at Yerevan State Conservatory with Albert Brutian. Between 1989 and 1991, he was a soloist with the Armenian Radio Symphony Orchestra and received the Grand Prize at the Armenian National Competition. Between 1991 and 1995, he studied at the Staatlichen Hochschule für Musik, in Freiburg, Germany, with Kim Kashkashian. During this period, he played under the direction of conductors such as Georg Solti, Valery Gergiev, Semyon Bychkov and Daniel Barenboim, and performed as a soloist with the Armenian Philharmonic at the Schleswig-Holstein Festival. He continued his studies at the Juilliard School in the United States of America, and completed a postgraduate degree at the Hochschule Karlsruhe. Later, he developed his artistic career with Professor Rudolf Barshai.

    Samuel Barsegian has participated in several workshops with conductors such as Bertrand de Billy, Simone Young, Gilbert Varga, David Zinman and Lawrence Foster. He is the founder and conductor of the Lisbon Chamber Orchestra and has directed several orchestras in Europe. In 2013 he first conducted the Gulbenkian Orchestra, in which he is 1st soloist of the violas.

  • João Tiago Dinis

    Viola

    João Tiago Dinis was born in 1987 in Aveiro. In 2007, while still young, he joined the Orquestra Filarmonia das Beiras, where he began his professional career. In 2023, he won a competition to become the B soloist for the Gulbenkian Orchestra’s viola section, which he still currently holds. He has also collaborated with various Portuguese and international orchestras such as the Kölner Kammerorchester, Orquestra de Câmara Portuguesa and, as first viola, the Orquestra do Festival de Marvão, Orquestra Clássica de Espinho and the Sinfonietta de Ponta Delgada, among others. As a soloist, Dinis has performed with the Orquestra Filarmonia das Beiras and the University of Aveiro’s Orquestra de Cordas.

    In the context of chamber music, he has collaborated with the Quarteto de Cordas de Aveiro, as one of its founders, and with the Quarteto da Orquestra Clássica do Centro.

    Dinis studied for a music degree at the Escola Superior de Música e Artes do Espetáculo do Porto (ESMAE) and at the University of Aveiro, where he won third place in the Frederico de Freitas Prize in 2017. He is regularly invited to give masterclasses and workshops at institutions around the country.

    Dinis plays a viola by Luís Claudio Manfio, “Isola Di Torcello”, from 2020 and a viola by António Capela from 2009.

  • Raquel Reis

    Cello

    Raquel Reis studied cello with Isabel Boiça at the Conservatório de Música de Aveiro Calouste Gulbenkian and completed her degree at the Academia Nacional Superior de Orquestra, where her teacher was Paulo Gaio Lima. She received first prizes in the Caldas da Rainha Interpretation Competition, the Samuel and Elinor Thaviu Endowed Scholarship Competition in String Performance (Northwestern University) and the Winnetka Music Club Scholarship.

    In 2007, she completed her Masters in String Performance at the Northwestern University School of Music in Chicago, with Hans Jensen. She was awarded scholarships by the Fundação para a Ciência e Tecnologia and the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation.

    Raquel Reis was a member of the European Union Youth Orchestra and the Spira Mirabilis Orchestra and has performed solo with the Gulbenkian Orchestra, the Orquestra Académica Metropolitana and the Orquestra Clássica de Espinho. She is a member of the Trio Pessoa, with which she recorded the CD Pessoa, dedicated to Portuguese music. She also recorded the CD of Portuguese and Brazilian music, Mundo Grande. She has been a member of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since September 2007.

  • Domingos Ribeiro

    Double Bass

    Domingos Ribeiro was born in Macao in 1992. He began his musical studies with Cristina Costa at the Calouste Gulbenkian Conservatory of Music in Braga. He graduated in 2013 from the Lisbon Conservatory, in Manuel Rego's class. He later studied at the Escuela Superior de Música Reine Sofía in Madrid with Duncan McTier and Antonio García Araque, with a scholarship from the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation and the Albeniz Foundation. He was an academician with the Symphonieorchester des Bayerischen Rundfunks, an orchestra with which he still works, collaborating regularly with Philipp Stubenrauch, Wies de Boevé, Heinrich Braun and Alexandra Scott. He also complemented his career by attending masterclasses or private lessons with Janne Saksala, Matthew McDonald, Rinat Ibragimov, Catalin Rotaru, Petru Iuga, Edicson Ruiz, Benedikt Hubner, Gary Karr, Iouri Axenov, Wolfgang Güttler, Hans Adler, Tom Goodman and others.

    He played in a number of youth orchestras, most particularly the Orchestre de Jeunes de la Méditerranée and the European Union Youth Orchestra, in both of which he was Section Leader. He has been guest reinforcement for Orquestra Sinfónica do Porto - Casa da Música in 2014, the National Orchestra of Spain in 2016 and the Budapest Festival Orchestra in 2017. In addition to these orchestras, he has also played with the Munich Philharmonic Orchestra, the Metropolitan Orchestra of Lisbon and Orquestra XXI, among others. He has worked with many conductors, including Mariss Janson, Bernard Haitink, Simon Rattle, Kirill Petrenko, Yannick Nézet-Séguin, Riccardo Muti, John Eliot Gardiner, Franz Welser-Möst, Kent Nagano, Ton Koopman, David Afkham, Krzysztof Urbański, Christian Zacharias, Alain Altinoglu, Lahav Shani, Matthias Pintscher, Christian Macelaru, Susanna Malkki, Carlo Rizzi, Peter Eötvös, Bertrand de Billy, Pietari Inkinen, Juanjo Mena, Peter Stark, Vasili Petrenko, Lawrence Foster, Michael Zilm, Brad Lubman, Michael Sanderling, Enrico Pomàrico, James Judd and Olari Elts.

    As a soloist, he has performed with the Lisbon Conservatory Symphony Orchestra and with the Camerata Gareguin Arantounian. He won the first edition of the Vasco Barbosa Competition in 2015, having performed solo at the Centro Cultural de Belém, with Camerata Atlântica, and recorded for RDP - Antena 2. In 2017, he was selected for the position of Leader of the Double Bass section - 1st Soloist - in the Gulbenkian Orchestra, a title he currently holds. He is in the 2nd year of his Masters in Music Teaching at Lisbon Conservatory. He is regularly invited to direct masterclasses and chamber music projects.

She has attended masterclasses by Christoph Schikedanz (Kissingen Sommer), Roman Nodel, Igor Oistrakh, Igor Volochine, Chistophe Poiget (Rencontres Musicales en Lorraine), Boris Kuniev, Daniel Rowland (Stift International Music Festival), Richard Gwilt (Baroque violin), Alexei Mijlin and Felix Andrievsky.

    During her formative years, she joined several youth orchestras, such as the European Union Youth Orchestra and the World Orchestra, and toured worldwide. She also played with the Orquestra Aproarte, Sinfonietta de Lisboa, Lisbon Chamber Orchestra, Orquestra Metropolitana de Lisboa and Orquestra de Câmara Portuguesa and played solo with the Orquestra Artave, the Filarmonia da Beiras and the Gulbenkian Orchestra. She has been a member of the Camerata Atlântica since its creation in 2013. She was a teacher with the Orquestra Geração. She has been a member of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2007.

  • Samuel Barsegian

    Viola

    A native of Armenia, Samuel Barsegian began studying violin at the age of six at the Tchaikovsky Special School of Music, but at the age of fifteen he decided to switch to the viola. He graduated in 1989 and then pursued his studies at Yerevan State Conservatory with Albert Brutian. Between 1989 and 1991, he was a soloist with the Armenian Radio Symphony Orchestra and received the Grand Prize at the Armenian National Competition. Between 1991 and 1995, he studied at the Staatlichen Hochschule für Musik, in Freiburg, Germany, with Kim Kashkashian. During this period, he played under the direction of conductors such as Georg Solti, Valery Gergiev, Semyon Bychkov and Daniel Barenboim, and performed as a soloist with the Armenian Philharmonic at the Schleswig-Holstein Festival. He continued his studies at the Juilliard School in the United States of America, and completed a postgraduate degree at the Hochschule Karlsruhe. Later, he developed his artistic career with Professor Rudolf Barshai.

    Samuel Barsegian has participated in several workshops with conductors such as Bertrand de Billy, Simone Young, Gilbert Varga, David Zinman and Lawrence Foster. He is the founder and conductor of the Lisbon Chamber Orchestra and has directed several orchestras in Europe. In 2013 he first conducted the Gulbenkian Orchestra, in which he is 1st soloist of the violas.

  • João Tiago Dinis

    Viola

    João Tiago Dinis was born in 1987 in Aveiro. In 2007, while still young, he joined the Orquestra Filarmonia das Beiras, where he began his professional career. In 2023, he won a competition to become the B soloist for the Gulbenkian Orchestra’s viola section, which he still currently holds. He has also collaborated with various Portuguese and international orchestras such as the Kölner Kammerorchester, Orquestra de Câmara Portuguesa and, as first viola, the Orquestra do Festival de Marvão, Orquestra Clássica de Espinho and the Sinfonietta de Ponta Delgada, among others. As a soloist, Dinis has performed with the Orquestra Filarmonia das Beiras and the University of Aveiro’s Orquestra de Cordas.

    In the context of chamber music, he has collaborated with the Quarteto de Cordas de Aveiro, as one of its founders, and with the Quarteto da Orquestra Clássica do Centro.

    Dinis studied for a music degree at the Escola Superior de Música e Artes do Espetáculo do Porto (ESMAE) and at the University of Aveiro, where he won third place in the Frederico de Freitas Prize in 2017. He is regularly invited to give masterclasses and workshops at institutions around the country.

    Dinis plays a viola by Luís Claudio Manfio, “Isola Di Torcello”, from 2020 and a viola by António Capela from 2009.

  • Raquel Reis

    Cello

    Raquel Reis studied cello with Isabel Boiça at the Conservatório de Música de Aveiro Calouste Gulbenkian and completed her degree at the Academia Nacional Superior de Orquestra, where her teacher was Paulo Gaio Lima. She received first prizes in the Caldas da Rainha Interpretation Competition, the Samuel and Elinor Thaviu Endowed Scholarship Competition in String Performance (Northwestern University) and the Winnetka Music Club Scholarship.

    In 2007, she completed her Masters in String Performance at the Northwestern University School of Music in Chicago, with Hans Jensen. She was awarded scholarships by the Fundação para a Ciência e Tecnologia and the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation.

    Raquel Reis was a member of the European Union Youth Orchestra and the Spira Mirabilis Orchestra and has performed solo with the Gulbenkian Orchestra, the Orquestra Académica Metropolitana and the Orquestra Clássica de Espinho. She is a member of the Trio Pessoa, with which she recorded the CD Pessoa, dedicated to Portuguese music. She also recorded the CD of Portuguese and Brazilian music, Mundo Grande. She has been a member of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since September 2007.

  • Domingos Ribeiro

    Double Bass

    Domingos Ribeiro was born in Macao in 1992. He began his musical studies with Cristina Costa at the Calouste Gulbenkian Conservatory of Music in Braga. He graduated in 2013 from the Lisbon Conservatory, in Manuel Rego's class. He later studied at the Escuela Superior de Música Reine Sofía in Madrid with Duncan McTier and Antonio García Araque, with a scholarship from the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation and the Albeniz Foundation. He was an academician with the Symphonieorchester des Bayerischen Rundfunks, an orchestra with which he still works, collaborating regularly with Philipp Stubenrauch, Wies de Boevé, Heinrich Braun and Alexandra Scott. He also complemented his career by attending masterclasses or private lessons with Janne Saksala, Matthew McDonald, Rinat Ibragimov, Catalin Rotaru, Petru Iuga, Edicson Ruiz, Benedikt Hubner, Gary Karr, Iouri Axenov, Wolfgang Güttler, Hans Adler, Tom Goodman and others.

    He played in a number of youth orchestras, most particularly the Orchestre de Jeunes de la Méditerranée and the European Union Youth Orchestra, in both of which he was Section Leader. He has been guest reinforcement for Orquestra Sinfónica do Porto - Casa da Música in 2014, the National Orchestra of Spain in 2016 and the Budapest Festival Orchestra in 2017. In addition to these orchestras, he has also played with the Munich Philharmonic Orchestra, the Metropolitan Orchestra of Lisbon and Orquestra XXI, among others. He has worked with many conductors, including Mariss Janson, Bernard Haitink, Simon Rattle, Kirill Petrenko, Yannick Nézet-Séguin, Riccardo Muti, John Eliot Gardiner, Franz Welser-Möst, Kent Nagano, Ton Koopman, David Afkham, Krzysztof Urbański, Christian Zacharias, Alain Altinoglu, Lahav Shani, Matthias Pintscher, Christian Macelaru, Susanna Malkki, Carlo Rizzi, Peter Eötvös, Bertrand de Billy, Pietari Inkinen, Juanjo Mena, Peter Stark, Vasili Petrenko, Lawrence Foster, Michael Zilm, Brad Lubman, Michael Sanderling, Enrico Pomàrico, James Judd and Olari Elts.

    As a soloist, he has performed with the Lisbon Conservatory Symphony Orchestra and with the Camerata Gareguin Arantounian. He won the first edition of the Vasco Barbosa Competition in 2015, having performed solo at the Centro Cultural de Belém, with Camerata Atlântica, and recorded for RDP - Antena 2. In 2017, he was selected for the position of Leader of the Double Bass section - 1st Soloist - in the Gulbenkian Orchestra, a title he currently holds. He is in the 2nd year of his Masters in Music Teaching at Lisbon Conservatory. He is regularly invited to direct masterclasses and chamber music projects.

• Beatrice Rana

    Piano

    At only 24 years old, Beatrice Rana is making waves on the international classical music scene, arousing admiration and interest from concert presenters, conductors, critics and audiences around the world.

    Beatrice performs regularly at the world’s most esteemed concert halls and festivals including Vienna’s Konzerthaus and Musikverein, Zurich’s Tonhalle, London’s Wigmore Hall and Royal Festival Hall, Paris’ Théâtre des Champs-Elysées, Lucerne’s KKL, Berlin Konzerthaus, Cologne Philharmonie, Milan’s Società dei Concerti, Ferrara Musica, Verbier Festival, Klavier Festival Ruhr, Lugano Festival, La Roque d’Anthéron Festival, Montpellier Radio-France Festival, Rencontres Musicales d’Evian, Enescu Festival, San Francisco Performances, Atlanta’s Spivey Hall, New Yorks’s Lincoln Center and Washington D.C.’s Kennedy Center.

    She collaborates with conductors such as Riccardo Chailly, Antonio Pappano, Yannick Nézet-Séguin, Fabio Luisi, Gianandrea Noseda, James Conlon, Emmanuel Krivine, Jun Märkl, Trevor Pinnock, Mirga Grazinyte-Tyla, Lahav Shani, Andrés Orozco-Estrada, Susanna Mälkki, Yuri Temirkanov and Zubin Mehta.  Orchestral appearances include the London Philharmonic Orchestra, City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra, BBC Symphony Orchestra, Philadelphia Orchestra, Los Angeles Philharmonic, Detroit Symphony Orchestra, NHK Symphony, Orchestre National de France, Tonkünstler Orchester, Lucerne Symphony Orchestra, Orchestra dell’Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia, Filarmonica della Scala, Helsinki Philharmonic and Royal Flemish Philharmonic.

    During the 2017/18 season, Ms. Rana plays recitals at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw as part of the Piano Masters Series, Cologne’s Philharmonie, Lucerne Piano Festival, Lisbon’s Gulbenkian Great Performers series and Toronto’s Koerner Hall, tours with Antonio Pappano and Orchestra dell’Accademia Nazionale di Santa Cecilia, Yuri Temirkanov and the St. Petersburg Philharmonic, Emmanuel Krivine and the Orchestre National de France, Osmo Vänska and the Helsinki Philharmonic, Sir Roger Norrington and the Camerata Salzburg, Gianandrea Noseda and Orquesta de Cadaques and returns to the London Philharmonic at the Royal Festival Hall with Mikhail Jurowski.

    The 2016/17 season will remain as a milestone in her career with the release of Bach’s Goldberg Variations on Warner Classics. The disc debuted at No. 1 on the U.K. Classical Charts and was praised by reviewers worldwide: in addition to being called “a supremely intelligent reading” by the Sunday Times, it garnered Ms. Rana Gramophone Awards Young Artist of the Year. She toured with the Goldbergs with concerts in Paris’ Théâtre des Champs-Elysées, London’s Wigmore Hall, Berlin’s Konzerthaus, Aix en Provence Festival de Pâques, Tokyo’s Toppan Hall, San Francisco Performances, Minneapolis’ Chopin Society, Porto’s Casa da Musica, Brussels’ Flagey, Birmingham’s Town Hall, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern Festival, among other major venues.

    Her first album as exclusive Warner Classics recording artist, released in 2015, featured Prokofiev’s 2nd piano concerto and Tchaikovsky’s first concerto with Antonio Pappano and the Accademia Nazionale Santa Cecilia di Roma. The CD received international acclaim including the prestigious Gramophone’s Editor’s Choice and BBC Music Magazine’s Newcomer of the Year Award.

    Beatrice Rana came to public attention in 2011 after winning First Prize and all special jury prizes at the Montreal International Competition. Her very promising career was brought to an even higher level in 2013 when she won the Silver Medal and the Audience Award at the 14th Van Cliburn International Piano Competition.  In September 2015 she was named a BBC New Generation Artist, and in April 2016 she was awarded a fellowship from the Borletti-Buitoni Trust.

    Born in Italy into a family of musicians in 1993, Beatrice Rana began her studies at the age of four and made her orchestral debut at nine, performing Bach Concerto in F minor. She achieved her Piano Degree under the guidance of Benedetto Lupo, her lifetime mentor, at the Nino Rota Conservatory in Monopoli, where she also studied composition with Marco della Sciucca. She later studied with Arie Vardi at the Hochschule fur Musik in Hannover and currently lives in Rome.

  • Ha Suyean Gayageum, Geomungo
  • Hwang Hyeyoung Gayageum, Geomungo

Coexistence

Drawing on two traditional South Korean string instruments, the gayageum and the geomungo, Ha Suyean and Hwang Hyeyoung created a duo that reinterprets the language of these instruments through a contemporary approach. Under the name Dal:um, the two young musicians invent a unique sound world, reclaiming tradition as living and renewable material through music that is as daring as it is beautiful, as enchanting as it is challenging. Their most recent album, Coexistence, was inspired by the natural landscapes around Seoul, but also by those they discovered during their European tours.

• Gulbenkian Orchestra

    In 1962, the Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation decided to establish a permanent orchestral ensemble. Originally with only twelve musicians (strings and continuo) it was named “Orquestra de Câmara Gulbenkian”. This collective was successively enlarged and today the “Orquestra Gulbenkian” (the name it has adopted since 1971) has a permanent body of sixty instrumentalists, a number that can be expanded depending on the repertoire.

    This structure allows the Gulbenkian Orchestra to interpret works from the Baroque and Classical periods, a significant part of 19th century orchestral literature and much of the music of the 20th century, including works belonging to the current repertoire of the traditional symphonic orchestras. In each season, the orchestra performs on a regular series of concerts at the Gulbenkian Grand Auditorium in Lisbon, where it has had the opportunity of working together with some of leading names of the world of music (conductors and soloists). It has also performed on numerous locations all over Portugal, in an effort to decentralize music and culture.

    The orchestra has been constantly expanding its activities in the international level, performing in Europe, Asia Africa, and the Americas. In the recording field, Orquestra Gulbenkian is associated to labels as Philips, Deutsche Grammophon, Hyperion, Teldec, Erato, Adès, Nimbus, Lyrinx, Naïve and Pentatone, among others, and this activity was recognized with several international prizes.

    Hannu Lintu is the Music Director of the Gulbenkian Orchestra since 2023.

items.content_html:
BUDAPEST - Flavescence dorée, a devastating grapevine disease, is spreading across Central Europe, threatening vineyards and the livelihoods of winegrowers.

The team's cross-border investigation examines how a threat identified by scientists years ago developed into a major epidemic – and why institutions failed to respond effectively while there was still time to contain it.

The team investigates what authorities in Hungary, Austria, and Romania knew about the disease, when they knew it, and what measures they took – or failed to take. The reporting looks at the capacity of authorities to monitor and contain the outbreak, gaps in surveillance and laboratory testing, the role of neglected and abandoned vineyards, and the incentives that may discourage growers from reporting infections.

The investigation also explores how climate change is contributing to the spread of the insect that transmits the disease, and how different approaches among winegrowers – from conventional chemical treatment to organic and more holistic practices – shape the response.

By comparing three countries at different stages of the epidemic, the project aims to identify the institutional and practical failures that allowed the crisis to escalate, as well as lessons that could help Romania and other countries prepare before the disease becomes even more widespread.

Methodology

The investigation combines cross-border investigative reporting, Freedom of Information requests, documentary research, scientific interviews and field reporting. The teams in Hungary, Austria and Romania are examining official records, surveillance and inspection data, legislation, institutional correspondence and government decisions, while interviewing scientists, winegrowers, industry representatives, officials and other relevant sources.

The three-country comparison is central to the methodology: rather than examining the outbreak in isolation, the team traces what authorities knew and did over time and compares institutional capacity, enforcement, reporting mechanisms and responses across countries at different stages of the epidemic.

Field reporting and audiovisual interviews are used to document the experiences of affected winegrowers and connect the institutional findings to the human and economic consequences of the disease.

  • Environment

Publication

ONLINE

More to come

  • Veszélyben a magyar szőlőterületek fele, a fitoplazma ellen minden gazdára szükség lesz, Qubit, 03/10/2026

  • Romania

Team members

András Tóth

András Tóth is an Hungarian staff writer.

Gergely Nagy

Gergely Nagy is a journalist and author from Budapest, Hungary.

Sarolta Kuglics

Sarolta Kuglics is a journalist based in Budapest.

Zsuzsi Kun

Zsuzsi Kun is an Hungarian multimedia journalist.

Tünde Szabó

Tünde Szabó is a Hungarian investigative reporter and editor in Romania.

Elisa Tomaselli

Elisa Tomaselli is a freelance journalist based in Vienna.

Related projects

  • © Berta Vicente Salas

    How Climate Change Threatens Some Wineries While Benefiting Others

    GOTLAND / MONTPELLIER – Is global warming making climate conditions less favourable for grape cultivation in southern Europe and more favourable in the north? The cross-border team conducted on-site reporting in four countries to see if this is true.

    Meer lezen
  • © Diana Dupu

    Industrial Pig Farming: Heavy Pollution Ends Up Green on Paper

    TIMOSOARA / SZEGED - Industrial pig farms report clean environmental papers, but nearby residents complain of odours and pollution, while groundwater shows nitrate contamination, and monitoring relies on self-reported data.

    Meer lezen
  • © Petru Zoltan

    Deadly Beaches: Tourists Drowned by Official Corruption

    ELENITE/MAMAIA - Mutilated by political decisions that generate huge profits for certain companies, the Romanian and Bulgarian beaches on the Black Sea have become graveyards for tourists who are left at the mercy of natural phenomena exacerbated by the authorities.

    Meer lezen

SAN PETERSBURG / ALESSANDRIA - Chemicals made in Russia keep crossing the EU to reach an Italian plant, despite the war in Ukraine and years of sanctions. Middlemen in Germany and Israel, trucks through Estonia and a price that rose eightfold kept the supply going.

Since February 2022, the European Union has adopted package after package of sanctions to cut trade with Russia. Yet one Russian-made chemical has kept travelling across Europe to a factory near Alessandria, in northern Italy.

The substance is 8-CNVE, a PFAS monomer used to make heat-resistant rubbers for aerospace seals and military vehicles. It is produced in St Petersburg by Anles, a company owned by the Kogan family and, according to import records, the only producer of this compound in the world. Its buyer in Italy is Syensqo, formerly Solvay, at its Spinetta Marengo plant.

The route is long and deliberately layered. The chemical leaves Russia in specialised leased containers, enters the EU through Estonia, crosses the continent by road and is sold through an intermediary: first Ftoran, registered at a private house in Birkenau, Germany, and from September 2022 Elastofluor, based in Israel.

The war did not stop the supply. From autumn 2023 the price of 8-CNVE exported to Europe rose to eight times its earlier level, a sign of a shrinking and riskier market, but Syensqo kept buying. In July, new EU sanctions targeting nitriles brought this kind of trade directly into question.

Across three episodes, this investigation reconstructs the supply chain, asks who knew where the chemical came from, and examines what companies along the route, and Italy itself, now risk.

Key findings

  • A PFAS monomer produced only in Russia, 8-CNVE, continued to reach Syensqo's plant in Alessandria after the invasion of Ukraine.
  • Shipments enter the EU through Estonia and cross Europe by road before arriving in Italy.
  • Sales run through intermediaries: Ftoran in Germany, replaced in September 2022 by Elastofluor in Israel.
  • The first recorded shipment to Alessandria dates from November 2021: 200 kg net, worth more than €230,000.
  • From autumn 2023 the export price to Europe rose up to eightfold, yet Syensqo continued to buy.
  • Syensqo registered 8-CNVE with ECHA in 2024 and filed the safety data sheet with local authorities in Alessandria around two years later.
  • New EU sanctions on nitriles, adopted on 25 July, raise questions about the legality of the trade and the responsibility of each company in the chain.

Methodology

The team began with trade data from the Import Genius database, searching shipping records under Anles's Russian company name. These documents list the supplier, buyer, intermediary, quantities, value and country of transit for each consignment. The team then cross-checked them against the ECHA registry, Italian local authority records, company registers in Russia, Germany, Estonia and Israel, and patent filings. The team reviewed confidential emails and carried out field reporting in Birkenau and Heidelberg, Germany, and along the Estonian–Russian border. The team then sent detailed questions to the companies involved, including Anles, Ftoran, Elastofluor, Syensqo, Arcese and Eurotainer, and interviewed experts on sanctions law and EU trade.

However, these sanctions did not affect most Russian fishing industries, which kept exporting 1.1 billion USD of seafood into Europe

From Jacques Ibert’s refined miniatures to the energy of Valerie Coleman, this concert, exclusive to Cartão Gulbenkian members, showcases the extraordinary versatility of the ensemble.

Through a series of short and contrasting works, soloists from the Gulbenkian Orchestra explore a sound world rich in colour, emotion, and rhythm, in constant dialogue between the instruments. An engaging programme that shows how chamber music, even in its most intimate form, can achieve the scale, intensity, and expressive power of a full orchestra.

Cartão Gulbenkian events have a limited capacity. If you are unable to attend, please return your ticket. Simply log in to your MyGulbenkian account, go to the “Tickets” section, and click “Cancel”.
